# Case Studies

> Teardown library extracted from **39 videos / 42 case studies** of Alex Hormozi's channel.
> Every figure below is traceable to a verbatim quote in the source transcript
> (audited: 1,305 of 1,305 numbers matched the transcript exactly).
> Quotes come from auto-generated captions — **numbers are reliable, wording is not**.

Framed as a study pattern: *how he reads a business, what he changes first, and what he leaves alone.*

**90 case studies · 3352 named mechanisms** across 516 videos.

## If You Hate Selling, Please Watch This...
`8VqSFBMMS4M` · https://youtu.be/8VqSFBMMS4M

*Scale or Fail teardown of Tina Sue's Hi Mama: convert the 3-4 hour founder-run 'Monday thing' into a 45-minute structured webinar with FAQ, reprice one-on-one at 5x, move the upsell to the halfway and two-thirds points, make it bi-annual so buyers opt out, add a 3-day no-sweat guarantee with same-day onboarding, and turn delivery Q&A into content - while the founder gives up answering every DM.*

### Case study

**Business.** Hi Mama - group program helping parents of children with autism, ADHD and speech delay (non-verbal kids to first words), delivered in cohorts via Telegram plus coaching team

**Starting state.** $770,000 revenue and $555,000 profit in the last 12 months (72% margin); core offer $2,500/year (3-month intensive + 9 months aftercare); upsell (all-access pass) taken by 10%; about 30% buy through checkout, the rest via DMs; converting about 9% on a 3-4 hour founder-run live 'Monday thing'; founder is in every Instagram conversation, all marketing and delivery; $150/month one-on-one membership with the coaching team; 200+ unposted testimonials; 7 employees (12 with coaches)

**Diagnosis.** The founder is the bottleneck and the conversion assets are unstructured: no formal webinar or FAQ handling, upsell only mentioned at the end, one-on-one underpriced, selling only to a warm audience, and an emotional block equating selling and charging more with being bad

**Intervention.**

- Replace the 3-4 hour marathon with a 45-minute structured webinar with slides: promise, quick story, who am I, core transformation (old way/new way), three biggest problems each handled as think -> why wrong -> what's right -> proof, then offer, then FAQ
- Answer the full FAQ live at the end of the webinar, in order of greatest percentage of questions, instead of one-on-one DMs
- Price checkout at $2,500 and one-on-one at $3,000 (the extra $500 framed as his $500/hour rate) to incentivize checking out rather than DMing
- Move the upsell into the intensive: sell at the halfway point, at two-thirds, and a last chance at the end - sell while they're mid-decision
- Make it bi-annual so the renewal is opt-out, not opt-in
- Add a 3-day no-sweat guarantee for the absent spouse, and onboard the next day to cut refund risk
- Run a weekly organic webinar for everyone who DMs (launches stay for the waitlist) and mop up the DMs
- Vibe-code an AI dashboard that searches past Telegram answers and suggests replies so the team handles delivery Q&A with more leverage
- Reprice or remove the $150/month one-on-one membership - one-on-one should be about 5x (8,000-10,000)
- Capture the 30-50 weekly delivery Q&As as bite-sized posts; green-screen answers for high-engagement questions; post the 200 testimonials
- Funnel every platform to Instagram DMs as the single conversion point, then to the webinar
- Run the content winners as ads, with a 3-second delay on the banner CTA

**Result.** She built the structured webinar; DM time fell from about 30 hours a week to three to five hours a week (down 90%); Alex judged 'you have scaled' and she advanced in the competition with a 12-month goal of 500 new clients

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Revenue and profit | **$770,000 / $555,000 (72%)** |
| Conversion before the fix | **9%** |
| DM hours before/after | **30 hrs/week -> 3-5 hrs/week (down 90%)** |
| Her 12-month goal | **500 new clients** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When the founder is the bottleneck: productize the pitch (structured webinar + FAQ), move the upsell to mid-decision, make renewals opt-out, put risk on the business with a short guarantee and same-day onboarding, convert delivery Q&A into content, funnel every channel to one conversion point - and accept the local cost of not answering every message.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Caption artifacts: 'bro marketing' as intended by the guest; '[music]' tags and '>>' speaker markers appear inside quoted spans; 'I did $770,000, and $555,000 is profit' is clean; 'bi-annually'/'biannually' spelled inconsistently in captions.
- The 9% conversion and 'double that' are his estimates for a warm audience; no post-intervention conversion number is given - the only measured result is the 90% DM-time reduction.
- The 'Monday thing' length (3-4 hours) is stated by him, not the guest.

## How to Sell Better than 99% Of People (4 HOUR ULTIMATE GUIDE)
`JE2_7elAcxM` · https://youtu.be/JE2_7elAcxM

*Four-hour compilation of his sales talks: sell with logic (three distortions - circumstances/others/self), obstacles vs objections, the CLOSER framework and the three things said on a call (questions, restatements, anecdotal stories), tonality/conviction (10% words / 90% delivery), the 8-step diagnostic sale with goal-tied pricing and prepay step-downs, a 60-day portfolio-company turnaround (56…*

### Case study

**Business.** Portfolio company he invested in (two-call sales process selling an ascension product to existing customers; founder had never sold) staffed by an outsourced sales team he calls 'mercenaries' taking 20% of revenue

**Starting state.** 20% of revenue going to the outsourced team as commission; less than 30% of buyers ascending to the next product; sellability/enterprise value at risk because a third party controlled 30-40% of revenue. Funnel per 100 front-end buyers: 74% show call one, 53% schedule call two, 63% show to the close call, 80% close = ~20 sales (20% of the front end vs the 30%+ he believed it should be). Mercenary closers cherry-picked only the easiest closes, setters de-qualified people too early, false urgency…

**Diagnosis.** Incentives were misaligned (mercenary closers optimizing dollars per hour, setters uncomped) and the close call had become a checkout page - 20% commission to take orders. He expected the funnel to be far better because these were existing customers with a card on file, not cold traffic.

**Intervention.** Five steps. 1) Hire one to hire 10: hired an in-house sales director - been-there-done-that, metric driven (quality and quantity of metrics correlates with skill), servant-leader demeanor, found through recruiters, content and outbound reaching 100-1,000 people. 2) Rebuilt comp: from 20% of revenue to sub-10% target, comped setters as well as closers, ratchets (50/60/70/80% close = job/attaboy/15%/25%), money plus not-money columns; landed at 9% all-in including the director. 3) Rebuilt the…

**Result.** 20% to 32% of the front end = 60% more sales for less than half the cost: $7M cash collected in Q1 at $1.4M commission (20%) became $12M the next quarter at $1.08M commission (9%); the ~$5.4M quarterly difference annualizes to $21.6M in profit (not revenue) because the customers were already acquired.

> **Transferable pattern.** Audit the funnel stage by stage and fix incentives before process; hire the one who hires the many; front-load obstacles before the price; and accept a lower close rate when the volume that reaches it multiplies - improve every number and let the throughput win.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Compilation video: the 4-hour guide reuses his other talks (the '9 things' list, the CLOSER/conviction training, the scaling-teams presentation, the diagnostic sale), so many quotes and numbers duplicate videos already extracted in this corpus (cy2k1GdA-9o, oi7bnS8uyJM) - this record keeps the…
- Auto-caption garbles kept verbatim in quotes: '211% increase' (=21%), '74 9991', 'paidon full'/'pifs' (pay-in-full), 'gam tape' (game tape), 'mning of nurture' (morning-of nurture), 'a dad within 14 days' (dud), 'no padas' (no special snowflakes), 'vssl' (VSSL), '36 Monon of Interest refinancing'…
- Multiple real businesses are worked through (three young founders 60-day turnaround; the brick-and-mortar chain diagnostic sale 14->32 locations; the mercenary-to-in-house swap) but the Tier B schema holds one case_study - the mercenary swap is used; the others are captured in numbers and stories.
- His throughput shorthand ('three and a half times more volume but we cut the close rate in half, so we increased total throughput') is directional: 3.5 x 0.5 = 1.75x, not the 'more than a double' he states; the $21.6M is stated as profit, not revenue.

## Hardcore Business Lessons I Learned From A Dealer
`vZfatNSouDQ` · https://youtu.be/vZfatNSouDQ

*Six lessons from a fifth-generation fur coat dealer: validate angry customers ('only one person in the angry boat'), invent a low-cost recurring 'insurance' product for the off-season, sell by getting people to say no, bait upsells with free 'sawdust', merchandise scarcity, and never stop doing the boring work.*

### Case study

**Business.** Fifth-generation fur coat dealer - retail store where he worked at 18 in the warehouse

**Starting state.** Coats sold for up to $25,000; no demand at all in summer; customers bought once and then price-shopped around town

**Diagnosis.** Nothing to sell in the off-season and no reason for a customer to return after the initial sale

**Intervention.**

- Sell a store-and-condition service on every coat: repair damage, sew, condition the fur so it lasts two-three-five times longer and can be passed to next of kin
- Price it with the car-insurance analogy: 'if you're going to buy a 50 000 car you'd pay a hundred bucks a month for insurance, it's the same thing here'
- Deliver it at near-zero cost - one 18 year old, two air conditioning units, three storage facility
- Use no-based selling on the phone: 'we're going to store and condition the coat, you don't want anything else do you' - the no implies yes to storage and conditioning
- Give away sawdust (fur scraps made into little purses and earmuffs) as a free bonus to get people in, then charge for the storage anyway
- Merchandise scarcity: no dealers allowed, 'limit two quotes per customer' sign, multiple strikethroughs to a 'final price', single-file line and fixed occupancy

**Result.** Doubled the number of coats people bought; customers returned every year for insurance and conditioning instead of price shopping; business survived five generations

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Price of the coats | **$25,000** |
| Coats bought per customer after the changes | **doubled** |
| Business lifespan | **five generations** |

> **Transferable pattern.** On a big one-time purchase, attach a cheap recurring service that gives the buyer a reason to return every year; fund the upsell with free byproduct bonuses, use no-based selling so the no implies yes, and let visible scarcity do the price holding.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Caption artifacts: 'coats' appears as 'codes'/'coach'/'quotes', 'angry boat' as 'angry bug', 'strikethroughs' as 'strike Downs'; the delivery-cost sentence and the $200M/year sentence are garbled - both recorded verbatim, not repaired.
- No revenue, margin or price-of-service figures for the dealer beyond the $25,000 coat price and the doubling of coats bought per customer.

## Give Me 42 Minutes, I'll Show You How To Sell Like The Top 1%
`zzleYxkf39k` · https://youtu.be/zzleYxkf39k

*A full teardown of a San Diego moving company: build a white-glove VIP tier out of components the competition never mentions (master movers, materials, insurance, a price cap, a same-day premium), sell VIP first and step down to standard, and win the realtor channel at brokerage level instead of paying $250 referral discounts.*

### Case study

**Business.** Flex 100 Moving and Delivery — a San Diego local moving company founded by Nass (29), with pink trucks, six employees, second-highest-rated mover in San Diego by Google reviews. 90% of revenue is local residential moves billed hourly ($165 for two movers plus $150 for truck and equipment).

**Starting state.** $300,000 revenue over the last 12 months at 62% profit. Leads come from Google Maps/SEO (~$1,000-1,200/month) plus realtor outreach offering $250 off moves over $2,000. Last month: 17 Google jobs produced $16,000, while 6 realtor jobs produced $15,000 — over $3,000 per job. He loses about 40% of deals to price. Goal stated as multiple locations at $2-4M each within 2-3 years.

**Diagnosis.** Not a lead problem — a sales process and packaging problem. Selling labour by the hour makes the business a commodity, so customers compare hourly rates with nothing else to talk about. The realtor channel was already showing the answer (richer customers, 3x revenue per job), but the referral offer paid cash back instead of using service as the incentive. Alex places him between stages three and four on the scaling roadmap: first full team, acting as manager, saying yes to every customer, needs product specialisation before scale.

**Intervention.**

- Rebuild the offer (fix back to front): create a VIP/white-glove tier against the standard tier.
- Stock the VIP with doubt-seeding components the competition never mentions: level-3 'master movers' (internal certification), all materials included, insurance, and a price cap.
- Charge a same-day surcharge of 10% (moving toward 20%) instead of avoiding the premium.
- Sell VIP first to everyone and step down to standard on 'I'm on a budget', then walk the seeds of doubt.
- Replace the $250 realtor discount with a free VIP upgrade for every client the realtor refers.
- Go after brokerages rather than individual agents: pitch the head of the brokerage for a brokerage-level deal, get integrated into their packet, and show up in person after the first response.
- Use AI to personalise the first SMS/DM to the 12,000-agent list; test a blue-bubble number against the generic opener.
- Add the foreman spiff to the review ask, and post before/after/review content to build local organic proof.
- Eventually hire one person full-time to farm the realtor relationships, and start refusing deals under $3-5K.

**Result.** No 90-day result is shown — Alex rules the business a 'fail' for the competition because multiple locations are too far off, while stating the plan itself will succeed. The owner leaves with the plan, orders a second truck, and puts his wife on the realtor relationships with AI. Alex frames the outcome as: fix the model before you scale it — 'he's in the nail-it phase more than the scale-it phase.'

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Revenue and margin | **$300,000 in 12 months, 62% profit** |
| Revenue per channel in one month | **17 Google jobs = $16,000; 6 realtor jobs = $15,000** |
| Revenue per realtor job | **over $3,000** |
| Deals lost to price | **like 40%** |
| Headcount | **six employees** |
| Same-day surcharge to introduce | **10%, moving to 20%** |
| Brokerage maths | **five houses a month = $15,000** |
| Deal size to eventually refuse | **under 3K or under 5K** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When you sell labour by the hour you are a commodity and price is the only variable the customer has. Rebuild the offer out of things the competition never mentions (vetted staff, materials, insurance, a cap, speed), present the premium tier first and step down, convert referral cash discounts into free upgrades of that tier, then sell the channel at the level where volume lives (the brokerage, not the agent) and use AI personalisation plus crew-asked reviews to keep the pipeline full.

## This Email Campaign Generates Sales [Full Breakdown]
`OpeN4O5myIg` · https://youtu.be/OpeN4O5myIg

*Full teardown of a 7-day challenge email campaign run to an unused list in one of his portfolio companies: 464,000 emails sent as a 15% test, 10,000 registrations at an 18% open rate, 800 buyers at $2,000, 20% ascending to the back-end offer, $2.4M in five days — then repeat the play to a different segment and run it quarterly.*

### Case study

**Business.** An unnamed portfolio company of Acquisition.com: a consumer business driven predominantly by paid ads, run like e-commerce (opt-in, then sale, then upsells), nine-figure annual revenue, almost $10M a month, multi-hundred-million-dollar enterprise value.

**Starting state.** A 3.3M email list collected over years that was used only for initial-transaction follow-up — 'after that they were dead to us'. Core offer $2,000 with a $88,000 back-end upsell; paid-ads CAC of $1,200 on the $2,000 item, leaving little margin. Ads then underperformed and quarterly revenue goals came under threat.

**Diagnosis.** The email list was an unworked asset rather than a constraint until ads softened. Because email CAC is $0 once the lead exists, every email sale drops straight to the bottom line, which both funds growth and lifts enterprise value.

**Intervention.**

- Promote a 7-day challenge to the list (the idea came from the marketing director, not the founder or Alex).
- Build the challenge from something the product already did for customers — pull it out and turn it into a lead magnet that completely solves one narrow problem.
- Send first to a test sub-segment: 464,000 emails, about 15% of the list, deliberately including many non-buyers, so a failure would not burn the whole list.
- Convert registrants into the $2,000 core offer, then ascend 20% of buyers into the back-end product.
- Rerun the exact same play to a different sub-segment a month later instead of waiting a quarter.
- After two validated tests, plan to run it to the whole list using the learnings, then repeat quarterly with a re-wrapped name and landing page.
- Split-test subject headlines, email openings, CTAs, links, landing pages, the offer and the challenge name; keep the core deliverable the same and change the wrapper seasonally or around a pain point.

**Result.** 10,000 registrations from the first send (18% open rate, ~5% click), 800 buyers at about 8% of registrants, $1.6M in new sales plus $800k from 20% ascending — $2.4M in total in five days, roughly $6 per email sent. The repeat run to a different segment produced $2.2M. Alex says the campaign added over $100M in enterprise value to a business already valued in the hundreds of millions.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Total revenue from the first campaign | **$2.4 million in 5 days** |
| Emails sent in the test segment | **464,000 (15% of the 3.3M list)** |
| Registrations and open rate | **10,000 registrations on an 18% open rate** |
| Buyers and conversion | **800 buyers, about 8% of registrants** |
| Ascension and its revenue | **20% ascended, an extra 800k** |
| Revenue per email | **roughly six bucks per email** |
| Second run result | **$2.2 million** |
| Enterprise value added | **over a hundred million** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When acquisition gets expensive, monetise the list you already own: pick a challenge that solves one narrow problem completely, send it to 10-15% of the list first, convert registrants to the core offer and ascend a fifth of them, then repeat the same play to new segments every quarter with a new wrapper and new tests — because the constraint was never the list size, it was that nobody had asked the list again.

## 10x Revenue with 1 New Sales Process (You Can Steal It)
`1UhvBSQFy6A` · https://youtu.be/1UhvBSQFy6A

*The diagnostic sale, end to end: pre-sale questionnaire to agitate the problem, credit card taken before the sale, current-desired-obstacle asked in the customer's words, price tied to the goal they picked, an incentive to prepay, and a step-down ladder ending in auto-recurring — installed in a 14-location brick-and-mortar chain that went to 32 locations with recurring revenue in the product line…*

### Case study

**Business.** A brick-and-mortar service chain he bought into roughly a year to a year and a half before the video — 14 locations at purchase, 32 at recording, with a med-spa-style product line (one-off treatments like botox or filler) plus memberships.

**Starting state.** The product line was doing $20,000 a month, of which 9% of revenue was recurring; there was essentially no membership option; customers averaged one extra visit (about two total); the average customer was worth about $200 and the only upsell was a ~$20 product. Lead generation and the core product were good — packaging was not.

**Diagnosis.** An offer and packaging constraint, not a core-business problem: they were selling one-off transactions and rebooking only if the customer called. The secret shop showed the reps collected the current state but never the desired state, never took card details up front, and priced the upsell at a tenth of customer value.

**Intervention.**

- Secret shop the business before buying (the sales director went in with a checklist: pre-sale questionnaire? card on file? current and desired state? what happened after the service?).
- Gather information and name the constraint — here, an offer/packaging problem: sell the solution and the goal rather than the service.
- Write the new sales process (four hours with the director of sales) and present it to management.
- Install the diagnostic sale: pre-sale questionnaire, credit card collected as 'setting up your account profile', current/desired/obstacle, then price tied to the goal.
- Kill the zombies — pre-handle the objections before the price is ever presented.
- Add a guarantee on the back end (e.g. keep working for free until the outcome is hit if they follow the steps).
- Offer a prepayment discount (20% prepay, 10% half down), then third-party financing, then a payment plan — and finally book the next visit if all else fails.
- Make the rebooking automatic so the payment plan rolls into recurring, and push membership.

**Result.** Recurring revenue in that product line went from 9% to 60%; memberships from essentially nothing to 30%; visits per customer from one extra (about two) to four to six; the product line went from $20,000 a month to over $250,000 a month in added revenue and kept growing. LTV per customer went 4x, from $200 to $800, and the chain grew from 14 to 32 locations in about 18 months — without changing what was delivered, only how it was presented.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Locations at purchase and at recording | **14 to 32** |
| Customer value change | **$200 to $800 (4X)** |
| Recurring share of the product line | **9% to 60%** |
| Membership penetration | **0 to 30%** |
| Visits per customer | **about two to four to six** |
| Product-line revenue | **$20,000 a month to over $250,000 a month in added revenue** |
| Upsell versus customer value found in the secret shop | **$20 upsell on a ~$200 customer** |
| Time to write the new process | **four hours** |

> **Transferable pattern.** You can multiply a business without changing what it delivers — only how it is sold. Secret shop to find the gap, collect the card before the sale, ask current/desired/obstacle in the customer's words, tie the price to the goal they picked, pre-handle objections before the price, then step down from prepay to financing to payments to recurring, and let the payment plan roll into an automatic charge. The same script ports across industries (gym, med spa, painter) because the constants are current state, desired state and obstacle.

## How I Scaled My Sales Team [Compensation, Recruiting & Training]
`okA9Yt2KZuk` · https://youtu.be/okA9Yt2KZuk

*How the sales machine was built and how the business was made sellable: a three-role org (BDRs making 100 dials a day for two shown appointments, SDSs who deliver value and set the close, BCs who close), a baseball-style promotion ladder with symbolic pay bumps and relegation, the beta process for replacing yourself as the product expert, and an outbound channel that went 1-2-4-6-8-12-16 sales a…*

### Case study

**Business.** His own business at the time — Gym Launch (gym licensing/education) plus Prestige Labs (supplements), sold after a two-and-a-half-year process; about a million a week in revenue and $17M profit in its second year when the exit process started.

**Starting state.** A big guru brand rather than a business: he was at the events, made the products and ran the coaching calls. Bankers, PE firms and network contacts named three weaknesses: churn, his name being the brand, and 100% channel dependence on Instagram and Facebook. A banker said they could get about 250 million if they finished the next 12 months at the same rate.

**Diagnosis.** Two structural weaknesses to fix before any exit: keyman dependence (he was inextricably linked with the brand) and single-channel dependence (Instagram and Facebook were 100% of sales volume). Outbound was chosen as the second channel because YouTube would not work in his niche, and because a manual channel cannot be switched off by a platform.

**Intervention.**

- Build a three-role outbound org: BDRs (100 dials a day in a four-hour shift, $50 per show, two shows a day expected), SDSs (45-minute call: 30 minutes delivering real value, 15 minutes setting the close), BCs as closers, plus a fourth team for ascensions.
- Scrape lists from Google and enrich them with VAs in the Philippines so the numbers and emails are real; dial through PhoneBurner with a local area code wrap.
- Use a value-first BDR script ('we just want to help you out') with an unscalable but genuinely valuable giveaway, then a scripted live handoff — call the closer on speakerphone in front of the prospect.
- Make the SDS's job to show expertise with two or three in-depth nuggets, then switch hats and set the close explicitly as a sales call.
- Build a baseball-style career ladder (junior/associate/[role]/senior at every level) with milestones roughly eight weeks apart, symbolic pay bumps, relegation on falling below qualifiers, and 'the ability to be promoted' at the top.
- Give promoted closers 10 deals in two weeks to prove themselves, dropping them back down if they miss.
- Replace the founder as product expert using the beta process: customers upvote problems, the top 1% (10-20 people) join a round table, notes are consolidated to only what all of them do, then the productised solution is tested on the bottom 10%.
- Introduce other people into the ads until it was just them, and take the name off the door (a three-year process) with siloed subject matter experts and customers-turned-heads-of-product.
- Restructure into shared services (IT, HR, legal, finance) plus profit drivers compensated on their own P&L growth, so leaders can earn 300-500k inside the company.

**Result.** Outbound went 1 sale in month one, 2 in month two, 4 in month three, then roughly 6-8, 12 and 16, reaching about 45 sales a month by month 14 — roughly 60% of total sales volume. Inbound close rate went from 20-25% to 60% because closers came up through outbound and were never spoiled with inbound leads. The business was sold after a two-and-a-half-year process; the offer was on the table the morning of this talk, and he says the decision would be aligned with what he is building next.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Revenue run rate at the start | **about a million a week** |
| Second-year profit | **17 million** |
| Banker's valuation estimate | **250 million** |
| Outbound ramp | **1, 2, 4, then 6-8, 12, 16 sales a month** |
| Outbound at month 14 | **45 sales a month, about 60% of volume** |
| Inbound close rate lift | **20-25% to 60%** |
| BDR cost per close | **$500 (at $50 per show)** |
| Close rate on scheduled appointments | **10%** |
| Beta process inputs kept | **180 items to five** |

> **Transferable pattern.** To make a business sellable you remove the two things buyers penalise — your face and your single channel. Build a farm-system sales org with a visible ladder (promotions every eight weeks, relegation on falling results), run outbound as a manual digital funnel with an explicit value-first script and a live handoff, and replace yourself as the product expert with a process (the beta process) rather than a person. Then decide whether to sell at all: match the post-sale conditions now, and if the industry will exist in ten years, refinance instead.

## If I Wanted To Grow An Audience In 2026, I'd Do This
`Jmkq5RLjm0U` · https://youtu.be/Jmkq5RLjm0U

*A four-talk megacut on building an audience and making money from it: the brand-pairing definition, the six content lessons with their measured lift, the agency playbook (hire a basic agency to force cadence, then a premium agency on a six-month learn-it-then-bring-it-in-house deal, then downgrade to consulting), the SPCL influence framework (status, power, credibility, likeness), and the four…*

### Case study

**Business.** His own YouTube channel, built by buying expertise from agencies before bringing it in-house.

**Starting state.** Zero subscribers, no knowledge of YouTube, TikTok, Instagram or Twitter, and no metric other than views. He describes a massive skill deficiency to overcome as fast as possible, and two ways to pay for it: time or money.

**Diagnosis.** The constraint was skill deficiency on a new platform, and the trap is hiring agencies on their terms - they retain you and put their best people on the newest customer, so results decay. His rule: no business owner should change their business for one client, so the engagement should be designed to end.

**Intervention.**

- Phase one - basic agency at about $3-5k/month whose only job was to force a three-videos-a-week cadence (trim the oohs and ahs, add intro and thumbnail) and teach the fundamentals for 3-6 months.
- Phase two - premium agency that works with top creators, on a six-month term: 'I want to do what you do in my business, but I don't know how. I'd like to work with you for 6 months so I can learn how you do it,' paying extra for the reasoning behind their decisions.
- Set a fixed deadline and tell them the plan: train the in-house team, then move to a lower-cost consulting agreement, so they can see the lifetime value ($6,000/month x 6 = $36,000 committed) and know the transition is coming.
- Document their process, co-create (they make for us and we make for us), and keep going until in-house output matches or beats theirs - the in-house team wins on time allocated and context, so only expertise is missing.
- Downgrade to consulting as insurance, and cut it one or two months later if the calls stop teaching anything - amicably, because the expectation was set up front.
- For TikTok, accept an agency's no-work offer to repurpose existing content, then buy the premium SOPs by hiring a director of brand who came from a premium agency.

**Result.** He says this is how he grew his YouTube, and that the method grew his audience by 5 million people in under 24 months from under 10,000 followers - with the same playbook later applied to LinkedIn, podcasts and paid ads. He frames the outcome as building enterprise value in-house rather than being dependent on a vendor who can raise prices once they see how much you make.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Basic agency cost and cadence | **$3-5k/month; three videos a week** |
| Premium agency commitment | **6 months; $36,000 committed at $6,000/month** |
| Audience result | **5 million people in under 24 months from under 10,000…** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Rent expertise on a deadline instead of subscribing to it forever: hire cheap to force the habit, hire expensive to learn the reasoning, document it, co-create until your team matches them, then downgrade to consulting and cut when the learning stops - and never let a vendor hold the asset your business depends on.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Compilation video: four separate talks stitched together (personal brand, the six content shifts, agencies/media team, influence and monetisation), with a results cold open. Large parts repeat three other videos in this batch (VQM3DrnVTcs brand talk, HVOubeXUcx0 six lessons, JOfsujnXxCg six shifts)…
- Internal contradiction on output volume: this video says '35,000 pieces of content this year' in the influence section but '35,000 posts over 40 months' in the six-shifts section.
- Internal contradiction on the book launch: '$105 million in sales in a weekend' in the cold open versus '$100 million in 72 hours or 3 days' later in the same video.
- Cross-video contradiction: Skool conversion figure is 30.44% here versus 33.44% in the other video in this batch that makes the same claim. The 30.44% figure is the one stated with the most context.

## She Turned 5800 Followers Into $1 Million Per Year
`0S5xsICW8qg` · https://youtu.be/0S5xsICW8qg

*A teardown of an anonymous registered dietitian who takes home just under $1M a year selling to other dietitians from 5,800 Instagram followers with 19 likes a post: one post and one story a day, all of it about the single niche, answering the audience's questions, one link-in-bio CTA every other post - plus his own two failed experiments with broad content, where views rose and every business…*

### Case study

**Business.** An anonymous registered dietitian's business teaching other registered dietitians how to bill insurance correctly and get credentialed - a coding/billing system plus low-ticket cheat sheets of billing codes and a higher-ticket offer.

**Starting state.** Just under $1,000,000 a year take-home (income/profit, not revenue). Marketing: 5,800 Instagram followers, average post 19 likes and about one comment, 30-day reach of 2,800 accounts, unverified account, 100% of acquisition from organic Instagram, email list of 2,900. Sales: 10+ low-ticket sales a day and about 3 high-ticket ($4,000-$5,000) sales a week.

**Diagnosis.** The constraint was not audience size and not views - it was relevance. Her entire audience was buyers of the one thing she sold, so a small room of the right people converted; the fix on his side of the table was the operational changes he mapped out with her, and the obvious account fixes she had not done (verification).

**Intervention.**

- One post and one story every day, with 100% of posts about the single niche (billing insurance as a registered dietitian).
- Make posts by answering the questions the audience asks - endless content supply.
- One call to action only: every other post says there is a link in the bio with more stuff you might like.
- Sell a low-ticket product (billing-code cheat sheets) continuously and a $4,000-$5,000 high-ticket offer about 3 times a week.
- Show up with full energy whether 8, 2 or nobody is watching.
- His stated to-do for her: pay for verification ($4.99 a month) and move the things around that they discussed, which he estimates takes the business to $3-5M a year in profit.

**Result.** Just under $1M a year in take-home income off a 5,800-follower account with 19 likes a post; he estimates $3M-$5M a year in profit with the changes, and uses her as the proof that niche content beats broad content.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Instagram followers | **5,800** |
| Annual take-home (income, not revenue) | **just under $1,000,000** |
| His estimate after the changes | **$3,000,000-$5,000,000 a year in profit** |
| Sales cadence | **10+ a day low ticket; ~3 a week high ticket** |
| High-ticket price point | **$4,000-$5,000** |
| First sale, on an email list of 8 | **$39** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Pick one specific person and one specific problem, post about nothing else every day, answer their questions, keep one link-in-bio CTA, and judge the business on business metrics (CPMs, opt-ins, sales) rather than views - a 19-like post is 19 real people, and 8 people on a list can buy.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The case is anonymous by design ('I'm going to keep it Anonymous') and he gives income, not revenue or list size at the start - the $1M is take-home and he explicitly says it is income/profit, not revenue.
- Caption corruption: '$4,000-5,000' prints as 'you know4 $5,000'; the email-list line prints as 'I've not I told 2,900 people on our email list'; acquisition.com prints as 'acis.com'; 'obious VI changes' (obvious fixes); 'regro dietician', 'underbuild', 'shatting this at myself' (chatting), 'many…
- The 1,000-true-fans idea is credited to a book whose author he says he cannot remember - he does not name it, so the record should not attribute it.
- The video contains a mid-roll sponsor segment (his community, caption prints the URL as 'school.com' / 'school.com s/ games') with an offer of a weekly call, a step-by-step course and 8 hours of monthly training - not part of the strategy.

## I Posted ONLY Business Content for 30 Days [STRATEGY REVEALED]
`JOfsujnXxCg` · https://youtu.be/JOfsujnXxCg

*The six shifts he made to his own content - edutainment to education, for-us to for-you, wide to narrow, views to revenue (ad revenue with RPM as the paired metric), shorts to longs, and assuming nothing about the viewer - and the measured result three to four weeks in: RPM up 68%, comments per view up 25%, subscriber conversion up 24.6%, opt-ins per week up 26%, book sales doubled and long-form…*

### Case study

**Business.** His own media operation: long-form YouTube, shorts and a podcast whose job is to feed Acquisition.com (workshop opt-ins, portfolio-company applications) and book sales.

**Starting state.** 35,000 posts over 40 months, a 7.8 million person audience, and content that had drifted wide (fitness, relationships, personal development), high-production and partly made for his own team; primary metric was views; about six months of wider content before the change.

**Diagnosis.** Four faults at once: content made for the team rather than the avatar; wide topics that pulled in people who will never buy; views as the only tracked metric, which rewards going wider; and content that assumed the viewer already knew him.

**Intervention.**

- Edutainment to education (education is defined as change of behaviour).
- For us to for you - make it for the business-owner avatar, not the team.
- Wide to narrow - business only.
- Views to revenue - make ad revenue the objective with RPM as the paired KPI.
- Shorts to longs - long form carries the buyers.
- Assume nothing - introduce yourself, no inside jokes, no warm-audience assumptions.
- Keep wide shorts as top-of-funnel brand awareness for retargeting.
- Operate on volume negates luck and never get the same scar twice.

**Result.** Three to four weeks in: RPM up 68%, comments per view up 25%, long-form views up 29.56% versus the six-week average despite fewer views per video, subscriber conversion up 24.6%, opt-ins per week up 26%, book sales 2x, applications up - and roughly 50 messages from founders (including $20-40M/year owners) welcoming the return of deep content.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| RPM change | **up 68%** |
| Opt-ins per week | **up 26%** |
| Book sales | **2x** |
| Subscriber conversion | **up 24.6%** |
| Long-form views | **up 29.56% vs six-week average** |
| Baseline | **35,000 posts / 40 months / 7.8M audience** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Run content as an experiment with a paired KPI: pick the narrow avatar, make the deepest useful thing for them, measure RPM and opt-ins rather than views, expect absolute views to fall while business metrics rise, and keep volume high so luck has somewhere to land.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Contradiction inside the video: he says a '7.8 million person audience' in the opening and later 'I built a 8 million personal audience' - the two figures do not match.
- Caption corruption: 'volume NE Gates luck' (volume negates luck), 'likes ain't cash views ain't cash is cash' (garbled), 'View use' (views), 'viws' (views), 'acquisition. comom' / 'a.com' (acquisition.com), 'school' (Skool), 'hi post production whizbangs' (high), 'Keynotes' (his own term for…
- The reported lift is measured only 3-4 weeks in, on his own channel, with no control - he says so ('I see this as anecdotal' for the comments metric, and 'this will compound' as a prediction).
- The '9% of people are business owners' and '.1% do $10 million a year' figures are his own sizing with no source.
- The book-sales doubling is described as '2x' with no baseline unit sales, and he notes the books sell every month no matter what.

## How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers
`Z2tgZC_XkT4` · https://youtu.be/Z2tgZC_XkT4

*The three-step Super Influencer Process - pick the right influencer (whose audience is bigger decides who brands for whom), get them to talk to you (verify yourself, the magic message, 100 messages a day), and close them (over-preparation with mockups and projections, promise-proof-plan, an offer so good it feels stupid to say no) - taught with the Nike/Jordan bet and a two-man UK team that added…*

### Case study

**Business.** Ms and Fahad - two men in their 20s in the UK with no following, no money, no ads and no product, who partnered with a former pro bodybuilder, Eddie Abbew, to build a paid community.

**Starting state.** Neither had an audience; Eddie Abbew had 50,000 followers and was in his 50s or 60s, and only wanted to make content. The product they built was branded around him (the Abbew crew) - getting people in shape and healthy again for a slightly older demographic.

**Diagnosis.** They had no audience to sell to, and the influencer had an audience whose want was more access to him. The constraint was not product or brand but who owned the audience and who was willing to do the operations.

**Intervention.**

- Reached out to influencers exactly as taught (the magic message), and got a reply.
- Told him he would be their only partner and only client.
- Offered to spend all their time growing his brand - taking him from 50k up, because that is what he cared about.
- Pitched a paid community with proof, promise and plan, and turned that into a presentation for him.
- Branded the product around him, not themselves.
- Took on everything he did not want to do: camera, recording, editing, posting stories, CTAs with links, and managing the community itself; he gets a cut of the money.

**Result.** In the first 30 days they reached $44,000 per month in recurring revenue in the US - which he calls top 1% income - with no ads and no following of their own.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Recurring revenue added | **$44,000 per month** |
| Time to get there | **first 30 days** |
| Partner's audience at the time | **50,000 followers** |

> **Transferable pattern.** If you have no audience and no product, go find an influencer who has the audience but does not want to operate: brand the offer around them, do all the work they will not do, give them the majority of the upside, and you can compress years of audience building into a few conversations.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Caption corruption: the editor-test result prints as '60 5% one in 20' (about 60 people, 5%, one in twenty); the Allen payout is fine but 'in Allen' is a caption artifact for the company name; 'acquisition. comom trining' (acquisition.com/training), 'school.com games' (Skool), 'febles'…

## How I Gained 7.8 Million Followers In 40 Months (6 Key Lessons)
`HVOubeXUcx0` · https://youtu.be/HVOubeXUcx0

*The six changes behind 7.8M new subscribers and 2 billion impressions in 40 months - edutainment to education, for us to for you, wide to narrow, views to revenue (RPM), shorts to longs, and assume more to assume nothing - with the five tactical levers for each (packaging, introductions, meat, visuals, pre-work), the proof-promise-plan intro formula, and the 90-day experiment where views went up…*

### Case study

**Business.** His own media operation across YouTube, Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok, X, Facebook, podcast and email - built to feed Acquisition.com (portfolio applications, workshop opt-ins) and book sales rather than to monetise directly.

**Starting state.** 40 months earlier: zero subscribers everywhere, a three-step plan (make as much good stuff as you can, post it everywhere, learn as much as you can), and views as the only metric. Over the period: $4M spent on team, equipment, vendors, studios and software; 1,000 hours on camera; 35,000 pieces of content.

**Diagnosis.** All views are not created equal. The channel was optimised for views, which rewards wider and more entertaining content, and the audience it attracted was not the audience that bought: a 90-day entertainment test tripled views and halved ad revenue, and a 10M-view video drove nothing while a 100k-view video out-earned it.

**Intervention.**

- Edutainment to education - all in on content whose point is to change behaviour.
- For us to for you - five tactical levers: vague to clear packaging, proof-promise-plan intros, language over razzle in the meat, effective production and data visualisation over effects, pre-search over post-production.
- Wide to narrow - business models, business leverage and selling, dropping relationships, college, food and lifestyle.
- Views to revenue - make ad revenue the metric, because RPM pairs quantity with quality and has near-zero latency.
- Shorts to longs - keep short volume but emphasise longs, which drive the conversions; shorts only carry cross-platform discovery.
- Assume more to assume nothing - introduce yourself, explain references, no inside jokes, talk to a stranger every time.
- Re-post the greatest hits and keep the intro the same with small variations.

**Result.** Over the 40 months: 7.8 million new subscribers, 2 billion impressions, 1 million books sold; platform-level: YouTube 0 to 2.23M, Instagram 7,000 to 2.5M, LinkedIn 0 to 324,000, TikTok 0 to 856,000, X 0 to 617,000, Facebook 0 to 25,000, podcast 3,000 to 25M downloads, email 0 to 700,000. He frames the six changes as saving the viewer the 3.5 years and $4 million.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Totals | **7.8M subscribers; 2 billion impressions; 1M books** |
| Cost of learning | **$4 million; 1,000 hours; 35,000 pieces** |
| YouTube growth | **0 to 2.23M subscribers** |
| Entertainment test | **views up 2-3x, ad revenue down by half** |
| Language vs razzle in top content | **75% of top performers emphasised language** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Pick the audience you actually want and make the content that changes their behaviour: clear packaging, proof-promise-plan intros, words over effects, data over flames, research before the shoot, one quality-paired metric (RPM-style) instead of views, long form for buyers, and an intro that introduces you every single time.

- This is the presentation version of the same six shifts covered in the 'I Posted ONLY Business Content for 30 Days' video (JOfsujnXxCg) - the two overlap heavily; this one adds the pre/post-work ratios, the 90-day experiment and the intro formula, that one adds the 3-4 week measured lift. They…
- Caption corruption in the platform numbers: 'My Tik Tok went from zero to $856,000 followers', 'my Twitter SLX ... went from0 to 600 17,000', '2 and a half million sub subscribers followers', 'LinkedIn went from Zer to 324,000', '25,00' (Facebook), 'N9 out of 12' (nine), '30 3.44%' (33.44%),…

## $100M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2024
`VQM3DrnVTcs` · https://youtu.be/VQM3DrnVTcs

*A three-part talk defining branding operationally as a deliberate pairing of things through an outcome - your thing, plus something your ideal customer already likes, plus the outcome they get - then showing why that pairing buys pricing power, better ad response and loyalty, and how to assemble and prune the pairings (a bouquet of flowers you curate, not a pile you happen to sit next to).*

### Case study

**Business.** Bud Light (Anheuser-Busch brand) - used as the worked example of a bad pairing and its repair.

**Starting state.** A mainstream beer brand whose core audience is conservative-leaning men; the brand ran an advertisement with Dylan Mulvaney.

**Diagnosis.** The advertisement was good advertising (everyone heard about Bud Light) but a bad branding pairing for their ideal audience: lots of people found out, and a lot of them hated it. The result was fewer people buying and a net loss for the business.

**Intervention.**

- Accept the bad pairing happened and cannot be removed.
- Pair the product with things the audience likes instead: the comedian Shane Gillis and the UFC.
- Let sales recover through the new, liked pairings.

**Result.** Sales began to recover. He gives no figures for either the loss or the recovery - the claim is directional only.

> **Transferable pattern.** Judge every partnership, sponsorship or spokesperson by whether the pairing nets more money from your ideal audience - not by how much attention it gets - and repair a bad pairing by overwhelming it with liked pairings rather than apologising for it.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The definition of brand is his own operational redefinition, explicitly built against the vague definitions he lists from other marketers ('if these sound vague and confusing it's because they are') - the record should not treat the pairing definition as the industry standard.
- The opening wealth claims ($200M/yr portfolio, $100M net worth, out-earning five named CEOs) are self-reported with no source.
- The $40 vs $10 Yeti comparison, the 12x price and the 0.5% / 6x click-through figures are illustrative examples he constructs, not measured results of a real campaign.
- The Buffett quotes are paraphrased from memory ('a quote from warff', 'another quote from Uncle warrant') and the caption mangles his name twice.
- The Bud Light case has no figures at all - no revenue loss, no recovery numbers - only the direction of the change.
- Caption corruption: 'school.com games.com trining' (skool.com, his Skool community), 'acis.com tring' / 'acc.com trining' (acquisition.com/training), 'braad', 'braining', 'braiding', 'bandic', 'herzi stuff' (Hormozi), 'preium', 'tactial'.

## A YouTuber Asked Me "How To Business". Here's My Answer
`4pZwlE86A5Y` · https://youtu.be/4pZwlE86A5Y

*A live opportunity analysis on Unspeakable's business: size each monetization vehicle by units times gross profit divided by competition, then do more of what already has the fewest unknowns rather than build the exciting new thing.*

### Case study

**Business.** Unspeakable - a YouTube creator business with 200 million monthly viewers, a 12-16 year old audience, merch, AdSense and brand integrations, plus a planned car shop and consumable product

**Starting state.** 10 years on YouTube, roughly 25 years old, three candidate monetization vehicles (media channel, car shop with parts marketplace, consumable/energy drink), 52 videos a year with the creator in every one

**Diagnosis.** Attention split across three vehicles; the media channel is the only one where he has no unknowns and the only one that scales, but it is capped by the creator having to appear in every video, and the brand is welded to one person who will age out of the persona

**Intervention.**

- Drop the marketplace idea entirely
- Keep the car shop, with the existing partner running day-to-day operations, and hire a junior to run its content
- Double down on the media channel as the main thing
- Find and rotate one to three co-hosts in so the channel can scale past the creator's own hours
- Build out the sponsorship bar on the existing audience
- Execute the phase-out plan for the creator over six to 12 months, ending in occasional appearances

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Monthly viewers on the channel | **200 million people every single month** |
| Current and target video output | **52 videos a year; could put out 100** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When an audience business has several possible products, rank them by unit economics divided by competitive density, then pick the one with the fewest unknowns - usually more of the media you already do - and remove the person as the single point of failure before the audience ages out of them.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The creator's 0 to 60 automotive shop and the parts marketplace are described but the transcript never states their revenue, so no figures exist for them.
- The '5x the sponsorship money' claim is Hormozi's assertion with no arithmetic behind it in the transcript.

## $100M Investor Answers The Most Important Business Questions for 1 Hour
`--9kOXNCUdE` · https://youtu.be/--9kOXNCUdE

*Nine business owners (from $200K to $140M a year) get diagnosed in sequence — in-network vs cash-pay economics, doubling an events business by running the same playbook twice, affiliate structures and their CAC math, guarantee sizing against refunds, valuation math on a $140M roofing roll-up, and solving one number (month-12 retention) in software.*

### Case study

**Business.** A roofing company ($140M revenue) that had just been acquired into a PE-backed platform of eight roofing brands; retail (non-insurance) model, 100% virtual sales with no in-home appointments.

**Starting state.** $140M revenue across the eight brands, ~$30M EBITDA, 40% gross margin, 10-15% net, eight tuck-ins assembled over three to four years; the owner is 30 days post-close and charged with combining the brands; his stated plan was to rebuild the offer (give away more, add guarantees).

**Diagnosis.** He said the offer was the constraint; Hormozi disagreed — the offer change touches every department and risks the whole book, while the obvious waste is sales: unproductive salespeople, leads lost to reps who cannot close, and duplicated cost from keeping reps on the road.

**Intervention.**

- Centralise all sales (already a condition of the acquisition) to cut cost and raise sales utilisation
- Cut the bottom third of the salesforce — the best reps absorb the volume
- Hire remote to widen the talent pool and get better closers at lower prices
- Only then consider offer changes, e.g. a profit guarantee on time and on budget instead of a money-back guarantee

**Result.** Predicted, not observed: he estimates the centralisation alone yields a ~25% lift in EBITDA, takes six months or more, and that the platform could reach $300-400M enterprise value on the existing $30M EBITDA before any offer change is risked.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Revenue and EBITDA of the roll-up | **$140M revenue, ~$30M EBITDA** |
| Predicted EBITDA lift from centralising sales | **~25%** |
| Guarantee alternative for high-hard-cost home services | **refund the 20% profit, keep the 40% gross margin** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Before changing the offer in an acquisition, bank the free EBITDA: centralise the function, cut the bottom third of the variable-cost salesforce, keep the top reps. The offer is the highest-leverage and highest-risk change — sequence it last.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Caption corruptions that matter for numbers: 'half at evida' (likely 'half EBITDA'), 'how many tukens have they done' (tuck-ins), 'in terms of business 6,000,000' where he then derives 12:1 from a $500 CAC — the $6,000 referral figure is corrupted in the caption, 'a lead magnet kind of which is…
- He computes 12:1 on the cellular therapy affiliate but never states the multiple formula; the caption's '6,000,000' would make the ratio 12,000:1, so the ratio and the figure contradict — treat the ratio as his stated claim and the referral value as unreadable.
- The $300-400M enterprise value implies a ~10-13x EBITDA multiple on ~$30M; he never states the multiple, so the implied multiple must not be recorded as a claim.
- Every business in this video is third-party: the revenue, margin, retention and price figures are the owners' own numbers as reported in the room, not Hormozi's.

## You're WASTING Your Chance to Make INSANE Money
`QTZsh3BgOwY` · https://youtu.be/QTZsh3BgOwY

*The six problems that stall a business — too many avatars, underpriced, overcompensation, overextension, growing for growth's sake and no data — each with the fix, followed by a full year of back-end data from a portfolio company that went from 5% to 30% profit by fixing retention and ascensions.*

### Case study

**Business.** A higher-ticket B2B portfolio company (acquisition.com) selling service in units — tens to just under 100 units a month — that he says had volume but a broken back end.

**Starting state.** Profit 5% of revenue, revenue retention ~2%, ascensions 0-1 per month, high employee churn, effectively no data: no engagement rates, no NPS, no customer start dates, no close rates by closer, no segments, no refund rates, no churn, no activation points, and a delivery leader actively turning the department against the founder.

**Diagnosis.** The product was good (buyers were happy) but the back end leaked: a cancerous CS leader, underpaid staff who could not be replaced with talent, no renewal or ascension process (100% of ascensions came from one superstar closer texting customers at random), and no data to see any of it.

**Intervention.**

- Hire a new customer-success leader who did not hate the founder
- Fire 90% of the baseline CS team and reboot the department
- Hire aggressively at better comp with benefits and 3+ years of experience, deliberately overlapping the two teams so the good people absorb the function
- Track the click-to-close funnel first (close rates overall, by closer, by period, by cohort), then the back end: time to value, time to onboarding, engagement, CSAT/NPS, ascension rates, churn and customer goals
- Build a renewal process: track time to value, install customer note history so customers never repeat themselves, reframe renewals around the customer's goals, and run the live events that historically produced renewals on a regular cadence instead of by accident
- Build an ascension journey with trigger points (immediate 24 hours, first value, halfway, milestone, last chance) and pay CSMs for sets and closers for closed sales

**Result.** Profit went from 5% to 30% (6x); revenue retention went from 2% to 30%; ascensions went from 0-1 per month to 5-6 per month; the back end added about $2 million in revenue that dropped almost entirely to the bottom line. He says it took no more than 90 days.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Profit before and after | **5% → 30%** |
| Revenue retention before and after | **2% → 30%** |
| Ascensions before and after | **0-1/month → 5-6/month** |
| Revenue added by the back-end fix | **$2 million** |
| Time to turnaround | **under 90 days** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Fix the back end before spending on acquisition: rebuild the CS function with better-paid, more experienced people, then make renewals and ascensions a choreographed journey (time to value, notes, goal-framed renewal, regular event, five upsell windows) rather than random acts by one star closer. He deliberately held ad spend flat while the holes were being plugged — spending more on a leaky bucket just compounds a bad reputation.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The Gym Launch activation-point figure is caption-corrupt: '$22,000 sale at a gym within their first seven days' is followed immediately by 'get the $2,000 sale in the first seven days' — the second statement is the coherent one.
- The portfolio company's revenue is never given, only its unit volume ('tens if not just under a 100 units a month') and the $2M added, so profit percentages are the only comparable figures.
- The six problems are presented as six but the fifth (multiple businesses) is folded into overextension rather than being a distinct diagnosis — the list is effectively five mechanisms with one doubled.
- The case-study figures are year-over-year as he states them, but he also says the changes were made in under 90 days — the reported stats and the reported timeline are not reconciled in the transcript.
- Third-party figures to keep separate from his own: Orange Theory's five-workout activation point, Carl Icahn's 11-floor story, Apple's 61 and Chick-fil-A's 58 NPS, and the 'average company' NPS of -2.

## How to Become Ultra Wealthy (4 Methods)
`BO_59sGxztY` · https://youtu.be/BO_59sGxztY

*Four capital structures for getting ultra wealthy - other people's money in your business (raise), your money in your business (bootstrap), your money in other people's businesses (invest), and other people's money in other people's businesses (run a fund) - with the fund-manager path shown to be the highest-leverage of the four and the reason private equity has created more billionaires than any…*

### Case study

**Business.** A private equity fund - the fourth path, other people's money into other people's businesses. Modelled on American Pacific Group, the $500 million fund that bought his own companies in 2021 for $46.2 million.

**Starting state.** A general partner wants to raise a $100 million fund. The GP contributes 5% - $5 million of personal capital, sometimes split across partners - because LPs want skin in the game.

**Diagnosis.** The GP's own capital is the scarce input, but it is not the productive input. The value of the vehicle is that the $5 million controls $100 million of LP capital, which levers into $200 million of debt, which buys $300 million of businesses - and the fee structure pays the GP on funds raised and on profit, with carry taxed as capital gains.

**Intervention.**

- GP commits 5% of the fund ($5 million) alongside $95 million from LPs
- Lever the $100 million with $200 million of debt to buy $300 million of businesses
- Charge a 2% management fee on funds raised annually - $20 million over a 10-year fund, before any investment outcome
- Take 20% carry on the profit at the fund's conclusion, taxed at capital gains rates
- Exit: sell the companies, repay the debt, return LP capital, then take carry on what remains

**Result.** Worked over 10 years: $300 million of businesses triples to $900 million. Less $200 million of debt, $100 million returned to LPs and roughly $100 million of interest leaves $500 million. The 20% carry is $100 million, which is $80 million post-tax. Add the $20 million of management fees and the GP turns a $5 million slug into $100 million plus over the period - and he notes that on a $2 billion fund you simply multiply by 20.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| GP contribution | **5% = $5 million** |
| Assets controlled per dollar of GP capital | **$5M controls $300M = 60x** |
| Fee structure | **2 and 20** |
| GP outcome | **$100 million plus on a $5 million slug** |
| The real-world instance | **APG: $1.2 billion AUM, bought his companies for $46.2…** |

> **Transferable pattern.** The highest-leverage capital structure is not owning a business or investing in one - it is controlling other people's capital invested in other people's businesses, because three layers of leverage stack on a small personal stake: LP capital on top of GP capital, debt on top of equity, and the acquired companies' cash flow on top of the debt. The GP is paid twice, once on assets raised regardless of outcome and once on profit, and the profit portion is taxed as capital gains. The prerequisite is not capital but access - proprietary deal flow plus an industry edge - which is why the same…

## No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026
`cnbHgYYHzyE` · https://youtu.be/cnbHgYYHzyE

*A year-in-review state of the union: three portfolio companies crossed $100 million valuation and portfolio EBITDA went from $50 million to just under $100 million, and the causes were narrowed to people, focus and conversion-rate optimization - with the single biggest personal lesson being that rush is imaginary and that problems, not missed opportunities, are where the money is.*

### Case study

**Business.** The media and conversion team inside acquisition.com - the division that produces his content and runs the acquisition funnel. He took direct control of it in the reporting year after about five years away from day-to-day operating.

**Starting state.** The division was meeting-saturated. In his own words he 'removed all meetings' as the first act, and every one-on-one he ran surfaced the same complaint: 'we're in meetings all day we hate being in meetings I just want to work.' Content creators are deep workers who need flow, and the meeting load was preventing it. The only route to advancement in the org was accumulating headcount, which incentivised hoarding talent and hiring requests.

**Diagnosis.** Not a talent problem and not a strategy problem - a coordination and incentive problem. Regular time blocks that did not increase output were consuming the deep work the function depends on, and the reward structure paid people for headcount and visible activity rather than for output.

**Intervention.**

- Deleted all recurring team meetings and one-on-ones; allowed ad hoc stand-ups only when solving a specific problem
- Replaced them with a single daily huddle, modelled on how sales teams are run because sales feedback loops are the tightest
- Installed the who/what/when framework: state the what, assign the who, and force the when by asking 'how many hours will this take' rather than 'what day'
- Recapped every item each time, so by the fourth item the first has been repeated four times and the last is freshest
- Added the 'say it back to me' version for teams that were not performing - he reports roughly one in three get it wrong
- Moved to pay for performance to the highest degree possible, after back-testing the new plan against the prior month
- On transition, let existing staff keep salary and added performance on top; new hires came in on performance only
- Built parallel technical and management tracks so the best individual contributors can earn more without managing people
- Removed people who were not aligned rather than training indefinitely

**Result.** Output more than doubled, with the expectation of reaching triple or quadruple. Separately, the largest portfolio company produced three CRO wins in the year - 20%, 50% and 28% lifts - off roughly 100 split tests run by one person and a couple of developers, at a company doing eight figures plus per month in revenue. Across the portfolio, EBITDA went from $50 million to just under $100 million.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Output change in the division | **more than doubled** |
| Speed gain from the timeline step | **7x** |
| CRO wins at the largest portfolio company | **20%, 50%, 28%** |
| Split tests behind those wins | **~100** |
| Portfolio EBITDA for the year | **$50M to just under $100M** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When a function is underperforming, delete before you optimise and optimise before you automate. Remove every recurring time block first and let the ones that matter be re-added by demand rather than assumed by habit. Then attach a time estimate to every task and pull it up, because unused bandwidth is not preserved - the future will not resemble today. Finally, change the reward structure, because the constraint is usually not capability but incentive: if the only way to advance is headcount, the org will manufacture hiring requests and manage for visibility instead of output. Back-test any…

## How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL
`k-3PoOT4vOM` · https://youtu.be/k-3PoOT4vOM

*Three unlocks for fast wealth: price off value created rather than cost incurred, structure the offer so customers prepay and finance the acquisition of the next customer inside 30 days, and understand that enterprise-value appreciation on a recurring base is tax-free until you sell - so the biggest tax strategy is to build something valuable and never cash it out.*

### Case study

**Business.** United Fitness - his own chain of gyms, opened with no capital by having customers prepay and finance each new location.

**Starting state.** $1,000 in his bank account in December 2016 after losing everything for the second time. No capital to fund buildouts.

**Diagnosis.** The binding constraint was capital, not demand. Once customer cash could be pulled forward to cover the buildout, the constraint moved to trainers, managers and salespeople - which is a hiring problem, not a money problem.

**Intervention.**

- Sold a six-week challenge rather than a membership, so cash arrived before delivery
- Ran paid ads at $5 per lead with a 1-in-5 close on a $500 product - $25 to acquire, $500 collected
- Put $5,000 down and signed a lease, then spent $100/day on advertising

- Reached roughly $100,000 collected by week four, covering the buildout plus six weeks of payroll
- Converted challenge participants into $20,000-$30,000 of recurring revenue per gym
- Repeated every six months with no money out of pocket

**Result.** Six locations by age 25, opened on a six-month cadence with essentially no capital out of pocket. The model was then productised: Gym Launch 1.0 charged $100,000 per gym on $1,000-$5,000 of ad spend, running 32+ launches in about 18 months; the licensing version went 0 to $10 million in sales in 10 months and did $26 million topline with about $16 million EBITDA in its second full year.

> **Transferable pattern.** When capital is the constraint, change the timing of cash rather than raising money. Sell a finite, outcome-shaped commitment (a six-week challenge) instead of an open-ended membership so the customer pays before you deliver; price the front-end so the first transaction returns more than the cost of the customer plus the cost of goods plus the cost of the next customer; and sequence the buildout so each week's collections fund the next week's spend. ## I Lost $100 Million... Here's What I Learned
`tdLLGKoBojo` · https://youtu.be/tdLLGKoBojo

*An itemised loss ledger of eleven of his own mistakes - crypto, an Ohio rental, nine failed partnerships, a bad partner who stole the account, fancy buildouts, food, software, vendors and a price cut - ordered roughly smallest to largest, ending with the pricing error that cost $5 million a year in profit and multiplied against his exit multiple.*

### Case study

**Business.** Hormozi's own portfolio of ventures over ~a decade: crypto, single-family rental, gyms, gym licensing (Gym Launch), a meal company, a software company (Allen) and various vendor relationships. Presented as a personal loss ledger rather than a balance sheet.

**Starting state.** By the gym-launch era he had roughly $20 million in cash from Gym Launch, six gym locations, and was making about $50,000/day in profit. Pre-2017 he had no investing experience outside of operating businesses.

**Diagnosis.** Every loss traces to one of two root causes: (1) operating outside his sphere of competence - crypto, real estate, food, software, where he had not developed skill; and (2) splitting focus off the core business, which had the highest return on his time. The single largest line item is not an investment loss at all but a pricing decision made reactively against a competitor.

**Intervention.**

- Stopped investing outside marketing/sales/acquisition/pricing/product; a mentor's rule - if you know how to create wealth, just create wealth
- Installed a FOMO pause: stop and say 'wait' when he feels the tickle of missing out
- Required any investment partner to have been in the deal 2-3 years minimum, and to co-invest alongside him
- Rebuilt partnership rules: partner must bring time, money or skills he lacks; equity need not be equal; the rainmaker gets a disproportionate share; owners working in the business take a salary
- Applied ROIC to every expense line, targeting 3:1 to 10:1 on dollars spent in a small business
- Adopted 'more, better, new' - doubling down on the main business instead of starting adjacent ones
- Hired a CFO and built one-layer-deeper reporting on every department so changes cannot happen without him knowing
- Vendor vetting: references at your exact size and use case, and treat personal referrals as strangers
- Switched from reactive competitor-watching to listening to customers

**Result.** Cumulative stated loss $100 million across the career. Named line items include $15 million on the vendor launch failure, $10-25 million on the food-business distraction (including the lost exit multiple), $5 million per year of profit permanently lost to the price cut, $1.2 million on delegated compliance, $1 million+ on outsourced software, $600,000/year on the unauthorised raise, $500,000 on crypto, and a $30-50k lesson from a single Ohio house.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Cumulative losses | **$100 million** |
| Largest single named loss | **$15 million** |
| Recurring annual profit destroyed by the pricing error | **$5 million/year** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Losses cluster into two repeatable causes that have nothing to do with market conditions: leaving the domain where you have developed skill, and diverting focus from the business with the highest return on your time. Both are self-inflicted and both are cheap to avoid - the discipline is a written rule about what you will not do, not better analysis of the thing you want to do. The corollary for pricing: never cut price reactively, because 20% off the topline at 40% margins is 50% of profit, and that recurring profit is what your eventual sale multiple is applied to.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Caption corruption: the Ohio flipper's purchase price appears as '$199,000' but the same sentence restates it as 'buy it for 19 flip it to 50' - the figure is $19,000, recorded verbatim and flagged rather than repaired.
- Caption corruption: 'now for a house that cost 5050' - this is '$50,000', restated as $50 elsewhere in the same passage. Recorded verbatim.

## How to make SO much money it makes you sick
`I64gYLBrics` · https://youtu.be/I64gYLBrics

*Strategy is prioritising, and prioritising starts with the constraint: find the one thing limiting the business, fix the unit economics before scaling the model, and order the work by impact and ease.*

### Case study

**Business.** A franchised multi-location food business, 20 locations, that came to Hormozi saying the franchise model was not working

**Starting state.** 20 locations - 6 corporate stores and 14 franchised. Average store cost about $1 million to open and made about $150,000 in profit per year, on about $1.3 million topline and $150,000 bottom line. A menu with 500 items. The owner had spent 10 years trying to scale the franchise.

**Diagnosis.** The constraint was not the franchise model but the unit economics - margins were below what the brand should command. In his words the sandwich was 'okay for the customer but it was terrible for the investor'. Scaling the model was multiplying a broken unit.

**Intervention.**

- Boil the 500-item menu down to the top 15 items everyone usually orders
- List all ingredients by type and renegotiate vendor deals by consolidating all demand for more volume
- Spend one month of each of the next 12 months finding 1% of profit back - 1% in month one, another 1% each month after

**Result.** Projected at the time of the conversation: after 12 months the business would be sellable, investable, and would have roughly tripled its profit. The framing he uses for the owner is a sellable enterprise rather than a job.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Locations and split | **20 locations; 6 corporate, 14 franchised** |
| Cost to open an average store | **about $1 million** |
| Average store profit | **about $150,000 per year** |
| Average store topline and bottom line | **$1.3 million topline, $150,000 bottom line** |
| Menu rationalisation | **500 items to 15** |
| Profit improvement cadence | **1% per month for 12 months** |
| Projected result | **roughly triple the profit and a sellable business** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When a multi-unit model is not working, stop scaling and audit the unit: the constraint is almost always in the unit economics, not the model. Cut the product line to the top sellers, consolidate purchasing to get volume pricing, then run a 12-month, 1%-per-month margin program. The 1% target is small enough to be achievable every month and compounds into a business that is investable rather than one that is merely bigger.
