## How to Get Rich for Service-Based Businesses (Thank Me Later)
`mRlSb0O5QNU` · https://youtu.be/mRlSb0O5QNU

*A 90-day teardown of an event-planning company: price the offer at 5-10x true cost with a dynamic quote sheet, add a price-lock and prepay discount, and turn the two underused salespeople into appointment setters for the owner.*

### Case study

**Business.** Utopia Experience - an event planning company in St. Louis run by Joey Goon (30 staff, 12 full-time), whose late mother founded it

**Starting state.** Average deal size $34,000 last year and $44,000 on a trailing-twelve-month basis, with quotes assembled ad hoc: a $15,000 retainer, about $15,000 of sponsor management and $7,500 of venue/logistics, with tiers added after a bad experience; the owner closed about 40% of calls at two appointments a week while his two full-time salespeople converted about ten times worse; he was also suing a client who filed for voluntary bankruptcy without paying

**Diagnosis.** Two linked constraints: the offer was mispriced against a cost basis he did not actually know, and demand was the real bottleneck. 'It's a margin issue... the pricing has to do with the offer, and so we kind of have to start with the offer and then fix price and then go sales motion and then go demand increase.'

**Intervention.**

- Cost out true costs by level of delivery - variable costs that scale with head count plus fixed costs (one person can only run four events, so her cost is a quarter of her salary per event)
- Price at 5x to 10x that cost, with 5x as the floor, in a dynamic quote sheet the team can use live on discovery calls
- Add a price-lock guarantee (scope fixed, head count allowed to move up to 20%) plus 10% off for prepaying
- Sell the whole year at once - ask 'how many events per year do you do?' on the call and quote all three, giving 10% off for committing to all three and another 10% for prepaying all three
- Build three VSLs (top of funnel, before call two, and post-event) so the call is spent closing rather than transferring information
- Reorganise the two salespeople into setters who prospect daily on LinkedIn and book discovery calls for the owner, with commission on what he closes
- Run daily team cadence (morning plan, mid-day lead prep, end-of-day pipeline) plus weekly one-on-ones that go personal, then short-term KPIs, then long-term goals
- Sponsor and speak at B2B conferences using a survey close to build the lead list

**Result.** The owner reports 200% more pipeline in booked discovery calls, a $15,000 booth sponsorship producing a $500,000 deal within a week, one-year clients converted to three-year clients, and nine out of ten prospects now sharing the same pain after narrowing the avatar. Hormozi's 90-day projection is one deal a week becoming two or three at $70-100K each, a $300-400K/month run rate.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Average deal size before | **$34,000 then $44,000** |
| Booth sponsorship result | **$15,000 spend producing a $500,000 deal** |
| Pipeline growth | **200% more discovery calls booked** |
| Target run rate | **$300,000-$400,000 a month** |

> **Transferable pattern.** In a services business with invented line-item pricing, cost out true delivery cost first, then price at 5-10x with the multiple set by the customer's wealth rather than the work. Lock the scope so the quote holds, then trade a 10% prepay discount for cash today. If the owner out-converts the sales team by 10x, do not train harder - convert the team into setters and let the owner close. And sell all the events the customer runs per year in one conversation, because tripling what they already bought is the cheapest LTV available.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- This is a Tier A-style teardown placed in the money tier; all of the company's figures (deal size, pipeline, the $500K deal, headcount, speaking rate) are third party - spoken by Joey, the owner - not Hormozi's own numbers.
- The $500,000 deal was still pending ('going to end up closing... within the next week') when the video was filmed, so it is a pipeline figure, not a closed result.
- The $300-400K/month run rate is Hormozi's projection for the 90-day competition, and the video does not show whether it was hit.
- The '25 of 100 events = 75% of profit' concentration figure is a prediction of what he expects the owner to find in a year, not observed data.

## How Acquisition.com Makes Money
`hHkdbr6_JJs` · https://youtu.be/hHkdbr6_JJs

*A full walkthrough of his own company's money flow: free media to email list to $9/month School and $30 books, into a three-tier advisory practice at $5K/$35K/$135K, with the cash redeployed into real estate and venture bets and a future $5-10K/year network membership.*

### Case study

**Business.** Acquisition.com (ACQ) - his own holding company: media, education, advisory practice, real estate, venture and private equity

**Starting state.** $250M+ portfolio; mission chosen after he and Layla sold their first company - make real business education accessible for everyone; they judged the gap as credible people not teaching business because they are busy running businesses

**Diagnosis.** Credibility is the scarce asset in business education, and the only people with more credibility than them mostly do not want to do the teaching - so the wedge is to give away the education and monetise the ascension

**Intervention.**

- Build free media, podcasts, YouTube and courses as the top of the funnel
- Convert attention into contact information via the Mosey Minute email list
- Add low-ticket conversion layers: books at about $30, School communities at $9/month
- Funnel converted traffic into the only high-value service: the in-person advisory practice at L1 ~$5,000 / L2 $35,000 / L3 $135,000
- Sell advisory almost entirely over the phone
- Redeploy revenue into ACQRE (multi-family real estate, partly for tax efficiency), ACQ Ventures (1-5% bets and seed-stage companies that can be sold through the distribution base), internal infrastructure, and private equity (30-100% stakes)
- Plan a scalable ACQ Network membership at $5,000-$10,000/year for 2026, with vendor pre-negotiation as the retention mechanism

**Result.** A working flywheel he summarises as: money from content, books, School (plus equity value and distributions), the advisory practice, and in future the network and ancillary services; target avatar is $500K-$50M revenue businesses

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Advisory tier prices | **$5,000 / $35,000 / $135,000** |
| School entry price | **$9/month** |
| Planned network membership | **$5,000-$10,000/year** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Give the education away free and make the free tier better than competitors' paid tiers, so credibility does the acquisition; then monetise only at the point where the buyer is already a business owner (here $500K-$50M revenue) and charge five figures for the in-person tier. Redeploy the cash into assets that are tax-efficient and that feed the same distribution base, and pre-negotiate vendor deals on behalf of the whole base so the network is cheaper to stay in than to leave.

## Making Money is a Game (Here's the Cheat Code)
`nSQdjim8CsE` · https://youtu.be/nSQdjim8CsE

*A money model is a deliberate sequence of offers - attraction, upsell, downsell, continuity - that makes a customer worth more in 30 days than they cost, with a fully worked gym example showing how the same 100 leads went from a $53/lead spend ceiling to $245.*

### Case study

**Business.** His own gym (large group training studio) - the money model that broke the gym industry, contrasted with the industry-standard $21 21-day trial

**Starting state.** $99/month membership with acquisition cost rising from about $100 to about $500 per customer; on a 10-month stay that meant paying $500 to make $1,000 and being cash-negative for five months; competitors ran a $21 21-day promotion and could spend at most $53 per lead

**Diagnosis.** The business was selling a commodity membership and hoping to recover acquisition cost over time, so the spend ceiling was set by lifetime value instead of by what one customer produces in the first 30 days

**Intervention.**

- Replace the $21 trial with a free six-week challenge (lower lead cost, higher motivation at the point of entry)
- Sell a $500 front-end package at the moment of greatest pain instead of a $21 trial - $7,500 cash upfront from 15 sales
- Add a classic supplement upsell in the first 48 hours - 12 of 15 at about $200, ~80% gross profit
- Add a rollover upsell: credit the $500 toward a year of membership, lifting take rate to about 70%
- Reprice the recurring membership from $99 to $250, discounted to about $200 for large group, with the credit applied
- Add a prepay discount at week six - 10% or 20% off for paying in full, taken by 20-30%
- Sell the one-in-five customer who buys something significantly more expensive (~$2,000 each)

**Result.** $24,500 from the same 100 leads versus $5,325 - a spend ceiling of $245 per lead versus $53, i.e. 5x; $19,500 of it inside the first 30 days, about $8-$9 back for every $1 spent, and the customer and the relationship retained for further sales

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Competitor spend ceiling | **$53 per lead** |
| His spend ceiling | **$245 per lead** |
| Return on ad spend, first 30 days | **$8-$9 per $1** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Raise the front-end price at the point of maximum motivation instead of discounting to a trial, then stack upsells at the moment of purchase (adjacent product), a rollover that credits the first payment toward a bigger commitment, and a prepaid discount - and price the recurring layer off the result rather than the market. The test of the model is not margin, it is whether one customer's first 30 days pays for the next customer's acquisition and delivery.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- This is a book-launch video: a large share of the runtime is promotion (the launch date, bonuses, the mystery gift, register.acq.com) and none of it is financial content.
- The gym model arithmetic is a worked example built on stated assumptions ('let's say'), so the $24,500 and $245/lead are his projections from his own experience, not audited results - and he explicitly says the prepay take rate is 'not a promise, not a guarantee'.
- The $80K/$130K supplement store figures are third party and he flags that he did not verify them.

## Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money
`hfwZwPGsbIo` · https://youtu.be/hfwZwPGsbIo

*A live teardown of a single mother running five businesses, plus his measured rule that every change costs about 20% of performance, so only risk-adjusted 20%+ improvements are worth spending one of roughly four change-shots per department per year.*

### Case study

**Business.** Kira's business - a publishing house with adjacent assets: five-day luxury book-writing adventures, an island retreat, an Amazon Prime TV show and a business school for women

**Starting state.** $1,000,000 in revenue last year; $1,000,000 already booked this year; she believes she is on track for $4,000,000 and hopes for $10,000,000; single mother of five; 'incredibly spread thin and overwhelmed'

**Diagnosis.** Not a capability problem - a focus problem. The adventures are not scalable, and the other businesses compete for the same audience; her market keeps pulling her towards books while she keeps trying to push the business school

**Intervention.**

- Identify which door customers keep knocking on - it is always the books
- Kill the other doors and go all in on the one with demand
- Use the Amazon Prime show purely as a media asset that pushes book writing, then sell more book writing
- Trade novelty for loyalty and stop launching new businesses

**Result.** No result is shown in the video - the intervention is the recommendation; Kira's own numbers before the change are the only figures

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Revenue before the intervention | **$1,000,000 last year, $1,000,000 this year to date, on…** |
| Largest single close | **$1,250,000 in five minutes to 30 people** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When several offers compete, find the door customers already knock on and remove the others - demand data beats your own vision of which business is more exciting. Then point every other asset (media, events, content) at that single offer instead of at the thing you want to sell. He applied the same rule to himself: nine businesses at a few million a year became one focused business.

- Kira's revenue figures are third party and self-reported on camera, including the 'on track for four' which is her projection, not actuals.

### Case study

**Starting state.** Growing and compounding, then flat: stuck at 30 locations for two quarters. Net receivables extended, and the CEO did not know how many locations the cash flow could support.

**Diagnosis.** Finance was the constraint of the business. The company had a bookkeeper who was not good enough and no operationalised finance function, so the CEO was operating blind on cash flow - not a demand problem and not a location problem.

**Intervention.**

- Name the constraint out loud to the CEO ('you are underdeveloped in the finance function')
- Replace the bookkeeper and build a real finance function
- Convert the accounting relationship from compliance reporting to fractional-CFO decision support - accurate, timely, broken down for decisions
- Only then set an expansion pace (his estimate: two or three locations a month)

**Result.** Not quantified in the transcript - he states the diagnosis and the expected unlock (two or three locations a month) rather than the realised result. He generalises that accounting firms should price on relating their numbers to the client's growth constraint.

> **Transferable pattern.** When growth stalls on a physical expansion plan, test whether finance is the constraint before assuming demand is. A business that cannot see its own cash position cannot be aggressive anywhere else, because it cannot be sure it is not bankrupting itself accidentally.

## Hard Money Lending EXPLAINED [I lent $3,000,000 using this]
`gxKxeie5JFo` · https://youtu.be/gxKxeie5JFo

*A completed $2.5M hard money loan teardown: 4%/month (doubling after four months) on a 334-unit Memphis building bought out of foreclosure, defended with personal guarantees, third-party offers, earnest money and title position - and the borrower caught a $75K error in Hormozi's favour and paid anyway.*

### Case study

**Business.** Private hard money loan - a $2.5M note to two buyers purchasing a 334-unit building out of foreclosure in Memphis

**Starting state.** $2.5M wired in cash; the building was basically condemned, in a war-zone area ('the police officers don't even go here'), with squatters and drug dealers; deal was supposed to close in 60 days and did not

**Diagnosis.** The risk is not whether the deal is good but whether the money comes back - so the structure has to answer 'what if I don't get repaid?' before the rate matters

**Intervention.**

- Take personal guarantees from both buyers, each with net worth in excess of $2.5M
- Evidence the building's value with three existing offers of $5M-$5.6M against a $2.5M basis
- Confirm $300K of earnest money already committed by the $5.6M buyer
- Get on title as the preferred position, paying off the prior lienholder, so no other liens exist
- Price at 4% per month ($100K/month) with the rate doubling to $200K/month after four months
- Insert a two-month minimum carry so the minimum fee is $200K regardless of timing

**Result.** A check back for $2.85M ($2.5M principal plus roughly $350K carry); about $175K after the 50% ordinary-income tax; he says he would lend the money out again at 10-20%

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Note size | **$2,500,000** |
| Monthly interest | **4% per month = $100,000/month** |
| Total repaid | **$2,850,000** |
| After-tax profit | **$175,000** |

> **Transferable pattern.** As the lender you write the terms, so structure the downside before negotiating the rate: guarantees with net worth above the note, independent third-party value evidence, money already committed by someone else, and title position with no competing liens. Then set a floor (minimum carry) and a step-up (rate doubles on delay) so delay pays you instead of costing you - and price the rate knowing the gain is ordinary income, not capital gains.

## My 7 year journey to making my first million.
`Xb9ZOA6zypU` · https://youtu.be/Xb9ZOA6zypU

*The unglamorous path to his first $1M of profit: fire-sell nine businesses, get a DUI, lose a partner's money, get cancelled by his payment processor with $100K frozen, and rebuild by switching from done-for-you gym launches to a licensing model he sold for $16K.*

### Case study

**Business.** Gym Launch - his own business, evolving from in-person gym turnarounds (done-for-you) to a licensing/consulting model sold to gym owners

**Starting state.** After the DUI he fire-sold five of six gyms and shut two agencies, putting the proceeds into the last facility where his partner then took the money out of the account; he was left with $23,000; the done-for-you model had a 35% refund rate and a ~20% margin, and he was burning $3,300/day across six simultaneous launches on a credit card with $1,000 of cash

**Diagnosis.** Two constraints. First, attention: nine or ten businesses meant nothing got enough of him. Second, model design: in the done-for-you launch he owned fulfilment but the gym owner owned the customer, so he could not control delivery, and every gym could poach his buyers with a refund-and-resign pitch

**Intervention.**

- Fire-sell the other businesses and go all in on Gym Launch
- Write refunds to everyone and pay the $22K commission on money never collected, to exit cleanly
- When the processor froze funds, find high-risk processors and stack them - one at $50K/month, then three at $150K/month
- When refunds spiralled, cut the middleman: write a sales letter in two or three days and sell weight loss online directly at $1,000/day all-margin
- Move the eight salespeople from gym floors to selling from home at $8,000/day
- Stop flying out: convert the launch model into a $6,000-then-$8,000 consulting programme, then call back the ~32 gyms already launched
- Repackage the same knowledge as a $16,000 licensing system (ads, copy, scripts, lobby layout) instead of $500K franchise pricing

**Result.** Refunds on the consulting version stopped because the product worked - the average gym collected $30,000 in 30 days, which produced word of mouth; monthly revenue went 100K, 300, 480, 780, then a million, 1.2, 1.5, 1.8, 2.2 million; $3M profit in the last four or five months of that year and $17M the next year; zero to $30M revenue in a year

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Refund rate in the done-for-you model | **35% of all sales** |
| Daily burn on six launches | **$3,300/day** |
| Result per gym from the consulting programme | **$30,000 collected in 30 days on average** |
| Licensing price | **$16,000** |
| Profit, that year and the next | **$3M then $17M** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When cash is the constraint, change the vehicle rather than the effort: the same skill set sold as done-for-you has low margin and no control, sold as consulting it has higher margin, and sold as licensed media it has no cost of reproduction. Own fulfilment AND the customer, or the channel in the middle will refund your sales. Stack processing capacity the way you stack offers. And when you shut something down, write every check - the clean exit is what lets the next model get sold.

## 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)
`bgBIO6nZawg` · https://youtu.be/bgBIO6nZawg

*Seven owners in a room doing $1M-$12M/yr get live constraint diagnoses — a neuropathy agency's rollup arbitrage, a lighting company with no revenue retention, a foreclosure-only flipper, a CPA firm with an onboarding gap, a SaaS with cohort churn, and a $10M Indonesian fashion brand being told to stop arbitraging media and build a brand.*

### Case study

**Business.** Permanent holiday lighting — LED track systems installed on homes and businesses, app-controlled, sold as permanent exterior lighting for holidays, game days and accent lighting. One location, Utah.

**Starting state.** About $1M in revenue at 51% margin (owner first said 60%), $5,000 average ticket, $300 CAC against a $5,000 LTV, roughly two years in business (the first year spent vetting products). Customers are a healthy split between elderly homeowners and people keeping up with the Joneses. No revenue retention: it is a one-time installation with no membership, subscription or maintenance plan.

**Diagnosis.** The constraint is not acquisition — $300 CAC against a $5,000 ticket is excellent. It is that the business has no repeat revenue and no data proving repeat behaviour, so it cannot be valued as anything but a one-time sale. He reframes the goal from recurring to reoccurring: reliable repeat purchases do not require a subscription.

**Intervention.**

- Run two to three seasonal campaigns a year (Easter, Christmas and a third occasion) to get back on site.
- Use every visit as an upsell moment — a maintenance check while there, then a pitch to upgrade to newer lights when the old ones age.
- Reframe the offer from 'recurring' to 'reoccurring': seasonal installs, maintenance fixes and upgrades, using Coca-Cola as the model of repeat purchase without membership.
- Instrument the data so the repeat rate is measurable and demonstrable to a buyer.

**Result.** No result is reported — the session ends with the target stated, not achieved.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Average ticket | **$5,000** |
| Margin | **about 60% as first stated, corrected to 51%** |
| CAC versus LTV | **$300 CAC, $5,000 LTV** |
| The retention benchmark that would re-rate the business | **half of customers buying something every year** |

## This video will make you more money than anything else on the Internet
`4GjwtnA76ig` · https://youtu.be/4GjwtnA76ig

*The offer is the strongest money lever: the same agency, mechanics unchanged, went from 0.5:1 to 11.2:1 return on ad spend (22x) purely by changing the offer, plus the leverage argument for selling to richer customers, the price-to-value discrepancy, and a live scarcity/urgency/bonus/guarantee demonstration.*

### Case study

**Business.** A generic Facebook Ads agency — 'thousand down, thousand a month, I'll run your ads for you' — the offer he uses as the canonical before/after.

**Starting state.** $10,000 a month of ad spend reaching 300,000 people; 40 booked calls; 75 appointments; 30 showed; 16 closed; 5 sales at a $1,000 price point — $5,000 collected on $10,000 spent, a 0.5:1 return on ad spend (reaching 1:1 by day 30).

**Diagnosis.** The offer was generic and interchangeable, so prospects compared prices and the agency competed on price against every other agency. Nothing about the mechanics of the business was the problem — only the offer.

**Intervention.**

- Change the pricing structure from $1,000 down plus $1,000 a month to $4,000 down as a one-time setup with no monthly fee.
- Move payment to a show-up basis: only pay when people show up.
- Make the guarantee implied rather than stated — if nobody shows up, they never pay again, which aligns the agency with the client's outcome.
- Change nothing else — not the fulfilment, not the media buying, not the funnel mechanics.

**Result.** Same $10,000 spend, same 300,000 impressions: 2.5x the response rate, 100 booked calls instead of 40, 75 appointments instead of 30, 2.3x the close rate, at 4x the price point — $112,000 of cash collected up front, an 11.2:1 return, described as 22 times as effective.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Old offer spend and return | **$10,000 spent, $5,000 collected — 0.5:1** |
| Old offer appointment volume | **40 booked calls, 75 appointments, 30 showed, 16 closed, 5…** |
| New offer terms | **$4,000 down, no monthly fee, pay on show-up** |
| New offer response and close rates | **2.5x response rate, 2.3x close rate, 4x price** |
| New offer cash collected and return | **$112,000 on $10,000 — 11.2:1, 22x as effective** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Before changing anything operational, change what the customer gets and how they pay for it. Moving payment to the moment value is delivered (pay-on-show-up) converts a price-comparison purchase into an aligned outcome purchase, and the price can then rise 4x while response and close rates rise too — the offer, not the delivery, is the highest-leverage variable.

- The new-offer funnel figures do not reconcile in the caption: it reads 'we went from five sales for ten thousand dollars 228 sales for ten thousand dollars', but $112,000 collected at the stated $4,000 price point implies 28 sales. The '228' is a caption artefact and is not silently repaired.
- 'ROAS' is captioned as 'row' throughout, and the response-rate description ('we got 100 though of points about rather than 40') is garbled — the 100-versus-40 booked-call comparison is the recoverable meaning but the sentence is not clean.

## KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.
`XwZH-lOKG9c` · https://youtu.be/XwZH-lOKG9c

*A four-part keynote - the math (client finance acquisition and 30-day cash), the offer, the traffic, and the money - whose capital argument is that a business funded by its customers' first-30-day cash needs no outside capital to grow, and whose biggest profit lever is price and the back end.*

### Case study

**Business.** His own gym (the first one), restructured around a free six-week challenge - the offer he then used to open six gyms.

**Starting state.** Could not sell a $99 a month boot camp; he says he could not even close people on a free trial; no cash to open locations.

**Diagnosis.** The offer was a commodity - a monthly boot camp price - so it could not produce the up-front cash needed to fund a lease, payroll and staff before recurring revenue starts.

**Intervention.**

- Replace the $99 a month boot camp with a free six-week challenge.
- Take $600 down, refundable on losing 20 pounds.
- Sell $300 of supplements 48 hours after purchase.
- At 21 days, offer the $600 back as credit toward a membership (12-month contract) - close 70-80%.

**Result.** Cost of acquisition dropped by a tenth and the business made 30 to 1 up front before membership dues, which funded six gyms in three years at 23 - 'completely full on someone else's money' before the first client showed up.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| The offer before and after | **$99 a month -> free six-week challenge** |
| Up-front return before membership dues | **30 to 1 up front** |
| Effect on acquisition cost | **down by a tenth** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Restructure the front end so the first 30 days produce more cash than acquiring and fulfilling the customer costs - free or discounted entry, money down, an immediate adjacent sale, then credit the deposit into a longer commitment. The up-front cash is what buys the next location.

## Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God
`hnfh2jqNVEQ` · https://youtu.be/hnfh2jqNVEQ

*What he took from two days next to Vista's former head of pricing - score every prospect and customer to find the vein of highest-LTV buyers, qualify the front end on the characteristics of the customers who win, set expectations from the average (not the outlier) and treat onboarding as the place lifetime value is decided - plus the Gym Launch numbers from applying it.*

### Case study

**Business.** Gym Launch - his gym turnaround/licensing company (he says 'we' throughout; the exercise runs on their own front end and customer base).

**Starting state.** Selling over 100 gyms a month with no front-end qualification; in the four weeks before the change, 22 escalations from the customers who were hardest to serve and got the least results.

**Diagnosis.** The wrong customers were the expensive ones: not gym owners, not full-time, no signed lease, no employees - they took the vast majority of the team's time and were worth less. Vista's method (score the pipeline, find the vein of highest-LTV customers) showed the best-customer profile was already in their own data.

**Intervention.**

- Pull a 90-day block of exits and escalations and score both ends: who made the most money, was easiest to work with, versus who left and escalated.
- From October, qualify the front end: at least 25 clients, a signed lease, full-time gym owner, ideally one employee or more.
- After a brief experiment selling a year up front with a 90-day sprint, switch back to the defined-end program.
- Point marketing and sales at the identified vein of customers and set expectations from the average and bottom-quartile results.

## 7 figure CONFIDENTIAL meeting LEAKED - business growth STRATEGY exposed...
`_8olk4-VFP8` · https://youtu.be/_8olk4-VFP8

*A live group-call teardown of a three-location gym owner who wants to franchise: the reason most licensing/franchise attempts die is unit economics too weak to sell, so fix the model and get one location to $40k/month without you before any franchise conversation - and open locations for pride, not for status.*

### Case study

**Business.** A multi-location gym operator (three locations, working on a fourth) in central California, not yet in a metro area, wanting to scale via licensing or franchising

**Starting state.** ~$100k profit total across three locations (~$30k/year per location) after ~$50k of one-time expenses; previously made $40k/month profit when he had one facility with three working owners plus small group and personal training

**Diagnosis.** Unit economics too weak to sell - "if you're doing 50 000 net per facility no one's interested in that" - and a rush driven by the desire to open more locations rather than to make the existing ones profitable

**Intervention.**

- Take a hard look at the other two locations; consider consolidating one into the other (move the EFT book, lose half of it, put all of it on the same fixed overhead) when the lease ends
- Get the remaining gym to $40k/month profit
- Keep it at $40k/month without being there at all, with an incentivised team
- Only then treat it as an asset on the balance sheet to sell, license or franchise

**Result.** Not reported in the clip - the video ends with the action steps and the operator agreeing; no outcome figures follow

> **Transferable pattern.** When a business plateaus, check whether the unit itself is worth replicating before choosing a vehicle for replication - and if one location made more money than three, the constraint is the model, not the market.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The case_study here is a live coaching call (a leaked group call), not a documented teardown: the business has no name, the result is not reported, and all figures are the operator's own statements on the call - marked third party in context.
- Cross-video conflict: this video and RBR4BwOVNvs both say the portfolio is "about 85 million a year", while other videos in the same batch say over $100M and over $250M.
- Caption artifacts: "aux mozy"/"mozi nation" for Hormozi/Mozi Nation, "the dave dunham throw punch", "the union economics suck" for unit economics, "eft" for EFT, "a zillion of them".

## How I Would Build a $10M Service Business (If I Had to Start Over)
`o64cI6tebnU` · https://youtu.be/o64cI6tebnU

*A 90-day teardown of Caleb's two-month-old St. Louis roofing company: Alex redirects it from chasing $18-25K replacements toward high-volume repairs, adds two VSSLs, a menu-close script, a maintenance membership and speed incentives - and revenue goes from under $32K to ~$250K in 90 days.*

### Case study

**Business.** Keys Roofing Company - premium and luxury roofing, gutter and downspout contractor in St. Louis, Missouri; owner Caleb, 2 months in business at filming (Scale or Fail episode)

**Starting state.** ~$41,000 revenue in the first 2 months (~$20K/month), $24,248 profit (~59%); one seller (himself); acquisition via door-knocking (20 doors ~ 1 sale) and referrals; average replacement ticket $18-25K; goal 7-10M in 3 years

**Diagnosis.** There is one of him and resources are constrained, so all effort must go to the highest-return move. The reliable money-getter (20 doors = a deal) is an asset; the cast-aside repair market is the opportunity - competitors won't even show up for small jobs, and repairs at $1,500/ticket and 64% margin can be systematized at volume. Constraint: salespeople (his stated blocker) and, per Alex's roadmap, specialization plus tracking as he scales headcount.

**Intervention.**

- Go all in on door-to-door as the primary growth engine ("DDD army"), violently - no being cute about it
- Specialize the product toward repair volume (and upsell roofs from there), systemize repairs
- Front-end VSSL: belief-breaking video with social proof shown on property before the sale
- Back-end VSSL about the maintenance membership, watched before the onboarding call
- Menu close script for Amanda: unsell -> prescribe -> fake choice -> card on file
- Maintenance membership ($15-20/month billed annually, $2 credit per $1 toward future repairs, discount for leaving a review) to convert one-time into recurring revenue
- Speed incentive (20% priority boost) to add margin on a supply-constrained calendar
- Treat salespeople as the new avatar - recruit and market to them

**Result.** 90 days later: revenue $250,000 (~$247K) vs a little under $32,000; 85 services built/sold/collected vs 32; 62 five-star reviews vs sub-20; repair services per month went from 15-20 to 60-80 (more than quadrupled); sales velocity more than 4x; repair tech at 3-5 services/day heading to 6-8 when a second tech joins. Alex summarizes it as "from 30K to 240K in 90 days".

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Revenue 90 days after the intervention vs before | **~$250,000 ($247K) vs a little under $32,000** |
| Reviews and services completed, before vs after | **62 five-star reviews (from sub-20); 85 services (from 32)** |
| Services sold per month under the repair model | **15-20/month -> 60-80/month (more than quadrupled)** |
| Repair services per day, now and after the second tech joins | **3-5/day -> 6-8/day** |
| Sales velocity change he attributes to going all in on door-knocking | **more than 4x the sales velocity** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Find the volume work competitors cast aside, orient the business to profit from it, get the first sale cheaply, then sell the adjacent thing (menu close) and convert one-time work into recurring membership - all funded by the one acquisition channel you are already reliably good at. Speed incentives add margin whenever demand exceeds capacity.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Caleb's 90-day numbers are self-reported on camera and slightly inconsistent in the same breath: 'I am at 250,000... it's like 247', and Alex's recap says '30K to 240K' - treat the jump as claimed, not audited.
- The '7K gross profit on replacements' figure is Alex's stated working assumption ('say 7K is gross profit on the replacements... Does that sound fair?') that Caleb agrees to - not a reported figure.
- The membership launch was still incomplete at the 90-day check-in - Caleb says he still needs a better sales motion for putting it on residential; the recurring-revenue piece of the plan was not yet proven in the results.

## This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners
`uaLNfijnp-8` · https://youtu.be/uaLNfijnp-8

*A 90-day consult case (Smile Magic Dentistry): the practice was supply-constrained, so the fix was offloading the simpler visits to associates, repositioning the dad as architect not operator, raising prices, shifting to pay-up-front, and speed-to-lead.*

### Case study

**Business.** Smile Magic Dentistry — a holistic dental practice in Orange County focused on implants, prominently for women; run by Hussle Nazir, who joined his father's practice about a year earlier (his dad is the only doctor).

**Starting state.** $2 million past-12-month revenue at ~47% profit (~$960,000); three locations but one doctor, so all high-ticket patients flow through the father and capacity caps at ~25-30 patients a month; diagnosis appointments booked 15-30 days out; only ~30% of treatment plans over $15,000 use financing; prices unraised for three to four years; goal $15 million revenue / $5 million profit in three years.

**Diagnosis.** Supply-constrained, not demand-constrained: the father does all five visits plus all diagnosis, so more marketing cannot add throughput. Secondary leaks: associates couldn't fill schedules, no VSL or sales education before consults, pay-as-you-go collections, and no speed-to-lead on paid leads.

**Intervention.**

- Offload the three less-skill visits to associate doctors — double the father's capacity from ~25 to ~50 patients a month
- Hire associates and reposition the father as architect/artist with the associates as hands (identity shift from best dentist to best teacher)
- Shift collections from pay-per-visit to pay-up-front: capture ID and card on file at intake, then 'credit card or financing' with a payment plan as the downsell
- Raise implant prices ~20% (average plan $28,000 to $44,000) and keep raising until conversion x price falls
- Add a VSL with testimonials shown before the sales consult — education as the second lever alongside qualification
- Speed to lead: respond in ~60 seconds; get new patients booked within 7 days instead of 15-30

**Result.** Observed at 90 days: two associates hired and all less-complicated work offloaded; revenue from ~$160,000 a month to on track for $500,000; average implant plan $28,000 to $44,000 with close rate up 3-4%; run rate $2.8M to $3.3M (~$270,000/month); new patients booked within 7 days and show rate up ~10%; no new locations needed yet.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Starting revenue and profit | **$2 million revenue, ~47% profit ($960,000)** |
| 90-day revenue result | **$160,000 a month to on track for $500,000** |
| Run rate at check-in | **$3.3 million, up from $2.8 million** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When the founder is the supply constraint: offload the founder's calendar to trained staff first, re-position them as architect (not operator), then raise price, prepay, and speed. Capacity doubles before a dollar more goes to ads — and the constraint usually isn't demand, it's the founder's beliefs.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- caption artifacts: 'Hussle'/'Husey' for the client's name (Hussle Nazir), 'DEXA rays' (X-rays), 'speed delete' (speed to lead), 'rigamarole', 'halfife' elsewhere in the batch; all results are self-reported by the client on camera 90 days later

## I Tried This Simple Business Strategy for 60 Days. This is what happened
`yPDQCfrwh8E` · https://youtu.be/yPDQCfrwh8E

*A data teardown of one portfolio company: he added ~$6M of enterprise value in 60 days by fixing the back end - pull time-to-first-value forward (47 -> 34 days), track and commission on leading indicators, and build a paid back end (ascension 10% -> 27%) - because solving a problem just creates the next problem.*

### Case study

**Business.** One of his 13 portfolio companies - a 16-week implementation program (the "three wise men" business from the earlier video); not named in the transcript

**Starting state.** Sales had just doubled (56 -> 93 units/month in 60 days) and fulfillment broke; time to first value was 47 days, customer satisfaction was untracked, the back end made $0, and churn was high - people were not making it through the 16-week commitment

**Diagnosis.** Three problems: (1) high churn - not delivering on promises; (2) no back end - nothing to ascend into after the first 16 weeks; (3) no metric tracking - two of three key stats did not exist

**Intervention.**

- Improve customer onboarding in four parts: sales/CS synchronicity with a formal handoff, track and pass on client goals, reset expectations after the paywall (and resell them on their why), set the outline of steps to the target
- Implement a CRM and KPI tracking - time to value and churn tracked automatically in real time, automated customer satisfaction surveys segmented by rep
- Commission the customer success team on the activation metrics and leading indicators (weighted by range: 100% -> 2x, 50% -> 1x, 0% -> 0x)
- Build the back end: a paid wall at the end of the 16 weeks (pay to stay), rolled out slowly to avoid shocking the system

**Result.** Time to first value 47 -> 34 days; customer satisfaction from untracked to 98% (he flags this as suspect - surveys went out right after the new onboarding); back end from $0 to $140,000 in 60 days; ascension 10% -> 27% in 60 days; ~$6M of Enterprise Value added

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| The commitment length of the program | **16 weeks** |
| Time to first value before and after | **47 days -> 34 days** |
| Customer satisfaction before and after | **non-existent -> 98%** |
| Back-end revenue created in 60 days | **$0 -> $140,000** |
| Ascension rate into the paid back end | **10% -> 27% over 60 days** |
| The enterprise value arithmetic | **$70,000/month profit -> just under $1M/year -> x6 multiple…** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Fix the back end before pouring more into the front: define the one activation moment that predicts retention, pull it forward (and re-communicate existing work so it is felt faster), track the leading indicators, tie commissions to the range, then monetize the next problem the first solution created - recurring back-end revenue is what gets multiplied in enterprise value.

## This Business Was Stuck. Here's How I Fixed It.
`4GQLJjH9-oA` · https://youtu.be/4GQLJjH9-oA

*Teardown of a portfolio company stuck at ~$570k/month for six months: 18%->24% webinar show rate, 58->102 calls booked, 14%->35% close rate, CAC halved to $2,868, and $860k/month past a $10M run rate in four months by pre-framing and communicating what they already did, not by adding new things.*

### Case study

**Business.** A portfolio company running a webinar-based offer: paid ads -> live webinar pitched by the founder once a week -> book a call -> phone sales team.

**Starting state.** About $570,000 per month, plateaued month after month for about 6 months. Webinar show rate 18% (he says it should be 25%+), 58 calls booked per webinar, sales close rate 14% (bad 'especially after a webinar'), CAC $5,763, LTV:CAC around 1.6.

**Diagnosis.** The constraint was acquisition — not enough customers. Underneath it: one weekly webinar slot meant a long gap between booking and show (people forget), the webinar lost a ton of people in the first minutes, bookings were weak because there was no takeaway/scarcity/proof, and sales had bad framing, meandering discovery, a feature-stack pitch, no roleplay and no granular KPIs.

**Intervention.**

- Marketing: 9-email pre-webinar sequence, simplified benefit-driven language, angles of pain / speed / ease / stuck-and-plateaued
- Added SMS, voicemail and video reminders so all four consumption channels are covered; the three most important reminders are 24 hours before, morning of, and one hour prior
- Behavior response: behind-the-scenes content to anyone who opened or clicked
- Webinar: faster intro using proof-promise-plan; say the date/time/weather to make the liveness obvious
- Takeaway: qualify exactly who it is for, state the real capacity constraint (only so many call slots) and first-come-first-served urgency
- Proof in the webinar: 'let me know in the chat when you book', call out bookings by name, call out sold-out times (Wednesday sold out, Thursday sold out)
- Sales: open by framing the call as qualifying for the guarantee (not everyone does) with B2B qualifications — business size, industry, owner; use BANT as the qualification
- Discovery: stay chunked up at the highest level humanly possible, avoid traps (details where both sides forget why they are there), never let the prospect take control of the conversation
- Pitch: pre-pitch invitation ('I think we'll be able to help you out... where do you want to go from here?') then a three-pillar pitch, chunking up a six-step process
- Execution: roleplay discovery with the team, track granular KPIs (show %, did you make the offer, which obstacle blocked), cut below-KPI closers' calendars in half with 1-2 weeks to prove out, best leads to best closers, and pay closers on cash collected

**Result.** Show rate 18%->24% (+33%); calls booked 58->102 (+77%); close rate 14%->35% (2.4x); CAC $5,763->$2,868; LTV:CAC to 3.96; revenue $569,000->$860k per month, past a $10M run rate and sustained; 30.7% profit margin, $250-300k/month profit versus previously teetering at the edge.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Emails in the pre-webinar sequence | **9 emails** |
| Close-rate lift at a larger portfolio company from rescripting only the first 5 minutes | **20% increase in close rates on a 3-hour presentation** |
| Closer commission difference between a payment plan and paid in full | **$200 vs $1,000 on a $110,000 sale (five payments of 2K, 10%…** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When a business is stuck, don't add new things: the constraint was acquisition, and the wins came from pre-framing the front of every step (webinar first 5 minutes, call framing), communicating what they already did (liveness, real capacity limits), keeping congruence down the whole pipeline, and measuring so the numbers themselves become the intervention.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Starting revenue figure is captioned '5 169,000' (probably $569,000, matching the opening ~570k/month) — recorded as captioned, not repaired.
- LTV:CAC baseline is captioned 'a 1.6 2' — ambiguous as transcribed.
- The upsell portion of this teardown is deferred to a separate video ('if it's not out yet check this one out').
- He says 'I didn't even lift it here because it wasn't worth doing' about call-booking-to-call-show rate — that metric is not given.

## Watch These 51 Minutes if You Want to Grow Your Business in 2026 (Dave Ramsey Interview)
`-HJg4TYBgtI` · https://youtu.be/-HJg4TYBgtI

*Hormozi interviews Dave Ramsey about how Ramsey Solutions is structured - 14 profit centers built over 35 years on 10% of ideas, in-person only, no equity and no exit - and Ramsey's most expensive failure: a debit card that was killed after several million dollars because the fraud risk was unbounded.*

### Case study

**Business.** Ramsey Solutions' failed product: a Ramsey-branded debit card (third-party case study told by Dave Ramsey, not Hormozi's own business)

**Starting state.** Several million dollars invested into building a debit card that was on-brand for Ramsey, with about 10,000 people in the beta. He says they did not know what they did not know about banking regulations.

**Diagnosis.** The product was not the problem - the risk was. Outside fraud bots began hitting the card, they had assumed the bank's software would catch it, and their contract made Ramsey responsible for the overdrafts being created. Ramsey's framing: the several million already spent was small compared to how bad the downside could get, because the losses could be infinite.

**Intervention.**

- Compare the sunk cost (several million) against the unbounded downside (contractual liability for overdrafts)
- Kill the product outright - 'we blew it up' - rather than protect the money already spent
- Accept the write-off and move on

**Result.** The card was killed. Ramsey adds that the bank they had been working with later 'went sideways and was in the news and blew up', which he reads as having exited the risk early.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Money invested in the failed debit card | **several millions of dollars into building a debit card** |
| The risk that ended it | **contractual responsibility for fraud-created overdrafts -…** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Judge a failing project on the downside, not the sunk cost. When a test shows that losses could be unbounded - here, contractual liability for fraud losses that the partner's software did not catch - kill it even if several million dollars are already in, because the money spent is small next to the worst case. Ramsey's secondary point: the partner he exited later blew up, which is what protecting the downside looks like in hindsight.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The video contains a full third-party failure case with numbers: several million dollars into a Ramsey debit card, ~10,000 beta users, killed because the contract made Ramsey liable for fraud-created overdrafts (unbounded downside), and the partner bank later failed.
- Ramsey gives a concrete idea hit rate and cadence - about 14 profit centers over ~35 years (one per ~2.5 years) built on about 10% of ideas, with 80-90% of new division leaders promoted from within - which is the operating system behind the 'test tube' advice.
- The five stages are given with names (treadmill, pathfinder, trailblazer, legacy - he skips one in the telling) and explicitly not mapped to revenue bands; the HVAC example (20 trucks, 70 employees) is used to show a business can still be stuck in an early stage.

## I Confronted a Stranger With a Failing Business...
`6Fg4VXjRphQ` · https://youtu.be/6Fg4VXjRphQ

*Teardown of a music-industry law firm losing $100K a year on $300K of revenue: kill the unprofitable software, point every traffic source at the channel that already works (Instagram DMs), stop billing by the hour, and sell the outcome at $5,800.*

### Case study

**Business.** A law firm for Latin-music artists and entrepreneurs (owner introduced as 'Alexi Omar' in the captions) with three units: legal services, education (courses/community), and a contract-template software product

**Starting state.** Last 12 months: $300,000 revenue and a $100,000 loss, with about 6 months of cash left. Services $131,000 revenue / ~$10,000 profit; education $131,000 revenue; software $40,000 revenue while burning $7,000/month (~$150,000/year cost). Distribution: 90,000 YouTube subscribers, 23,000 Instagram followers, 800 new Instagram followers a month, a website doing 7,000 visits and 150 leads (2% opt-in), 9 of 150 buying a $500 course plus $500 upsell. Services were billed at $250/hour (about 524 hours…

**Diagnosis.** Focus and monetization, not demand. He was running three businesses and splitting one source of eyeballs across three destinations, two of which lose money - the education is effectively a charity and the software costs $150,000 a year to make $40,000. Meanwhile all the actual revenue came from Instagram DMs, a channel he never promoted. The profitable unit was underpriced and hourly-billed, which both caps revenue and misaligns incentives, and he had no qualification, no video sales letter and no price anchor.

**Intervention.**

- Kill the software (drawn as a red X): either sell it to the interested B2B buyers at cost or shut it down; the education stays but is reframed as a charity/long-term lead nurture, not a profit centre
- Point every traffic source at the one channel that already works - 'DM me on Instagram' - in four places: a 30-second CTA at the 30% mark of every video, the description above the fold, a pinned comment, and the profile
- Make the DM the funnel: have them book a call without paying; the free 'consultation' is explicitly a sales call, preceded by a 5-7 minute VSSL that sets expectations and shows proof
- Qualify before the landing page on BANT plus income (not Spotify stats): 10 million artists on Spotify but only 1,000-2,000 are professional
- Stop billing hourly: sell the outcome at $5,800, with a $25,000 no-commission alternative as the price anchor, plus the 5% on deals
- Downsell unqualified or lower-intent leads to the education product at $2,000-$3,000 instead of $500-$500 - a phone call typically triples the price of the same thing
- DM every new follower with 'are you here for free content or do you want help?' - 800 new followers a month, close 5%, that is 40 extra sales a month at $6K = $240,000
- Give the book to unqualified leads as an elegant long-term relationship play; use the education community (Skool rather than Kajabi) to generate free onboarding calls
- Enforce delivery economics: at least 80% gross margin, meaning cost under about $1,100 on a $5,800 sale (under 11 hours at $100/hour)
- Price speaking engagements at opportunity cost: 3 sales a day at $6,000 over 2 days = $36,000 plus travel, because demand is not the constraint

**Result.** No after-numbers - the video ends with the owner agreeing to the plan ('Will you do this? Yes.'). Hormozi's projections: $240,000 a month from the new-follower DM play alone, $18,000-$50,000 a day with three sellers at a $6,000 offer, and the next constraint becoming supply (running out of lawyers) rather than demand. He also says he does not know if the client will reach $1M a month from this.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Starting state | **$300,000 revenue, -$100,000 profit, 6 months of cash** |
| Software drain | **costs $150,000 a year and makes you 40 [thousand]** |
| Price changed to | **$5,800 outcome-based price** |
| Projected result of the DM play | **40 more sales a month at 6K, about 240 [thousand]** |
| Margin rule | **80% gross margin minimum, cost cap ~$1,100 per $5,800 sale** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Run the audit in this order: (1) kill or sell the unit that loses money - do not fund a fantasy while the cash runs out; (2) find where the money actually comes from today (here, unpromoted Instagram DMs) and point every existing traffic source at it instead of fixing the channel that never worked; (3) qualify hard before the sales call (budget, authority, need, timing) so the seller's time is only spent on people who can buy; (4) replace hourly pricing with outcome pricing and set a price anchor above it ($25,000 vs $5,800); (5) downsell everyone who does not qualify to a cheaper product at…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The diagnosis is arithmetic and checkable: the software costs $150,000 a year to make $40,000, the education is break-even once separated, and the only profitable unit ($131,000 services, ~$10,000 profit) was the one being neglected - that is what turns a $100,000 loss into a fixable problem.
- The pricing move is specific: from $250/hour to a $5,800 outcome retainer with a $25,000 no-commission anchor, plus a repriced $2,000-$3,000 education downsell, on the rule that a phone call typically triples the price of a checkout-page sale.
- The delivery economics rule is quantified here and usually omitted: 80% gross margin minimum means the cost of delivery must be under about $1,100 on a $5,800 sale, i.e. under 11 hours at $100/hour of lawyer time.
- Speaking-fee math is given as opportunity cost: 3 sales/day at $6,000 over 2 days equals a $36,000 minimum fee plus travel.

## The first 5 hires EVERY entrepreneur should make...or go broke...
`7NqsFh5ej0w` · https://youtu.be/7NqsFh5ej0w

*Hire in reverse order of the value you personally provide (and the market cost to replace it) - admin, customer support, sales/setter, marketing assist, fractional bookkeeper, then IT - while choosing which type of debt you incur as you grow.*

### Case study

**Business.** His own portfolio companies (Acquisition.com, gym/fitness businesses) used as the reference case for sequencing the first hires

**Starting state.** Early-stage business where the founder is doing everything; administrative work, support, sales, marketing and finance all sit on the owner

**Diagnosis.** The constraint is the founder's own time and the debt the business accrues while growing. Two debts matter: replacing skills in the wrong order (expensive skills first) and letting CRM, bookkeeping, people and management gaps build up, which then have to be paid back with interest at larger scale.

**Intervention.**

- Hire in reverse order of the value you provide and the marketplace cost to replace it: (1) administrative help, (2) customer success/support, (3) first salesperson or setter, (4) marketing assist/prospecting or videographer, (5) fractional bookkeeper, and often a sixth IT/tech person
- Do not take these as hard and fast rules - shift sales earlier if sales is not your strong suit, later if you are a killer closer
- Choose which debt to incur: use financial debt (investment) to incur less operational, talent, CRM and management debt
- Ascend each early hire over time into a director/manager with a team hanging off them

**Result.** He claims the strategy of choosing financial debt over other debts is why each subsequent company grew bigger, faster and stronger than the ones before it, because they could skip the stages (new CRM, fixed financials, better management) that normally set a business back a quarter to a year.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Revenue below which a fractional bookkeeper is sufficient | **$100,000 a month** |
| Annual revenue of Acquisition.com's portfolio | **$85 million a year** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Sequence your first hires by dollars-per-hour math, not by org chart: replace the cheapest, lowest-value-per-hour work first (admin, support), keep selling and marketing yourself while those are your highest-value hours, and take fractional help (bookkeeper, lawyer, tech) rather than in-house until scale justifies it. Then explicitly pick which debt to incur - paying for infrastructure and talent early (financial debt) is cheaper than paying back CRM, financial and management debt with interest later.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Written summaries list the five hires but omit the two thresholds he gives here: the ordering rule is explicitly reverse of value-per-hour, and the fractional bookkeeper is stated as sufficient below $100,000/month of revenue.
- The debt taxonomy (life, management, financial, technological) is presented as a portfolio-level strategy - he says his later companies grew faster because he deliberately took financial debt to avoid the other kinds.

## I Built a Business That Runs Without Me
`EdUAAVKl_io` · https://youtu.be/EdUAAVKl_io

*The jump from rich (doing the right things) to wealthy (owning the right things) is made by delegating not only the job you do now but the next job you would have learned - hire someone who already has that skill and keep only ownership.*

### Case study

**Business.** Hormozi's own two fitness businesses inside the Acquisition.com portfolio - the worked example of active income becoming ownership income

**Starting state.** 2018: $17M profit from the two businesses, with him doing everything in them

**Diagnosis.** He was getting paid for what he did, not for what he owned. The degree to which he had personally grown the business capped it, because he only ever delegated one step ahead and kept learning the next skill himself.

**Intervention.**

- Delegate the job you are currently doing to someone else
- Instead of learning the next job yourself, find who already has that skill and give them the next job too (jump two steps)
- Interview candidates to learn the role and hire people who know more than you do
- Keep ownership of the business rather than doing the work inside it

**Result.** He now does nothing in those two businesses. Profit went from $17M (2018) to a projected $8.1M this year with COVID for half the year, yet the businesses are 'more valuable now' than when he did everything. On a $8M base, a 20% return means going to $9.6M next year, which he calls ridiculously easy now that he can assemble rather than build.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Profit from the two fitness businesses in 2018 | **$17 million** |
| Expected profit for the same two businesses this year | **$8.1 million** |
| Return target and the growth required | **20% / $8 million to $9.6 million** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Do not delegate one step at a time. At each step, hand over both the job you do now AND the next job you would have learned, to someone who already has that skill. You get the same growth curve the business had when you ran it, but you keep only the ownership. Corollary test: if you are the one doing the highest-value work in the business, you own a job, not a business - and your own skill level caps the business at the size you can personally run.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Generic 'who not how' summaries say to delegate what you do; Hormozi's version here goes one step further - delegate the NEXT job too, to someone who already has the skill - and he prices the cost of getting it wrong with real numbers ($17M profit in 2018 with him operating vs $8.1M projected with…
- The claim that a business is worth MORE when the owner is absent is asserted without a valuation multiple, only by the profit swing and his stated 20% return requirement.

## Building a $1,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 26 Minutes
`HGZOxBfnF-E` · https://youtu.be/HGZOxBfnF-E

*Teardown of Luis Lora's railing e-commerce store: the constraint is broken attribution plus the wrong customer mix, so fix the data, pick the DIY segment you already own, and route every product through a one-step funnel that closes custom orders on the phone.*

### Case study

**Business.** Optimum Works - Luis Lora's online railing store (homeowners, contractors, designers; 70% DIY, 30% custom orders; Shopify)

**Starting state.** $2.5M revenue, $384K profit, 15% net margin, LTV:CAC reported as 1:1 (and 0.41:1 in the ads data). 81% of customers from Google Ads; $21.6K/month on Google and $4.5K/month on Meta; over $300K of marketing spend last year with CAC doubled. ~10% repeat buyers. AOV $873. 10,000-person email list. 5-year-old business, full-time for 2 years. Goal: 10x revenue, double profit.

**Diagnosis.** Two constraints, neither of which is traffic. First, attribution is broken - an LTV:CAC of 0.41:1 is impossible in a profitable business, so no spend decision can be optimized; the agency is likely taking credit for referral traffic. Second, the customer mix is wrong: he is serving contractors and designers who are price sensitive and treat him as a commodity, when 70% of the business is DIY buyers who are less price sensitive and most obsessed with the product. Fix the data, then reorganize the business around DIY + custom.

**Intervention.**

- Fix attribution first (stop trusting the post-purchase survey; find which campaigns actually work), then move spend from the losing campaigns to the winners
- Reposition as 'the home for DIY railings' and optimize for DIY + custom rather than contractors and designers
- Put the custom-order flow on every product, not just the best sellers, and make the 'custom designs available' banner sticky
- Build a one-step funnel: form + calendar in one step, then a 5-7 minute pre-call VSL (hook, proof, promise, plan, picture) covering materials, price ranges and delivery expectations
- Nurture by SMS before the call to capture BANT (budget, authority, need, timing), and frame the call as 'you are going to buy on this call'
- Close on the call: A/B choice of credit card vs financing, plus a $200 discount for moving forward on the call to avoid extra calls
- Raise prices on the DIY range (AOV $873 toward $1,000) because the segment is far less price sensitive and margins are thin
- Run long-term nurture in parallel: 2 emails per week to the whole 10,000-person list (one before/after, one FAQ/offer rotation), delegated to someone else
- Order of operations: build the system first, then drive traffic, then use the script, then add nurture

**Result.** One year later (filming April 2025, follow-up March 2026): $3.6M revenue and $540,000 profit, +44% revenue growth. Custom orders went from 30% to 50% of the business - the single biggest driver of profit. Close rate is 20% with triple the number of custom-order leads submitted. Fixing attribution revealed campaigns that were only breaking even, so money was moved from losers to winners; prices were also raised. Owner's words: 'The advice that made the biggest difference was optimizing for…

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Starting revenue, profit, margin, LTV:CAC | **$2.5M / $384,000 / 15% / 1:1** |
| Revenue and profit in the 12 months after the teardown | **$3.6M / $540,000** |
| Revenue growth over the year | **44%** |
| Custom orders as share of business after the changes | **50%** |
| Close rate and custom-order lead volume after the changes | **20% close rate, 3x submissions** |
| Attribution problem - reported LTV:CAC | **0.41 to 1** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Fix the measurement before buying more traffic, and fix the customer mix before optimizing the funnel. Concretely: (1) if the reported LTV:CAC is arithmetically impossible for a profitable business, the attribution is broken and no spend decision is real - repair it and move budget to the campaigns that survive; (2) pick the segment you already have the most of that is least price sensitive and most obsessed, and re-aim the whole business at it instead of serving the most price-sensitive buyers who treat you as a commodity; (3) route every product through a one-step funnel (form + calendar,…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The one-year follow-up numbers are the most valuable part and are usually missing from summaries: revenue $2.5M to $3.6M (+44%), profit $384K to $540K, custom orders 30% to 50% of the business, close rate 20% with 3x custom-order leads, and prices raised after attribution was fixed.
- He explicitly refuses to give a long list of tactics - only two or three highest-impact changes - and gives an order of operations (system, then traffic, then script, then nurture in parallel), which the framework summaries compress into generic funnel advice.
- The specific price test is stated numerically: the $873 average order could be raised to $1,000 with little loss because the DIY segment is not price sensitive, and DIY projects could reach $1,300-$1,500.

## I Blew Up A Secret Business To Prove It's Not Luck
`SmiOK8Yun4s` · https://youtu.be/SmiOK8Yun4s

*Teardown of a fashion stylist doing $309K a year: fix the leaky funnel (lead magnet, VSSL, harder qualification, headline), scale the affiliate channel she was ignoring (6 partners already produced a third of revenue), and reprice with a high-end anchor and a default back-end.*

### Case study

**Business.** Ashley's fashion styling business - personal styling and design advice for high-income clients (CEOs, socialites, frequent flyers) with a $8,500 60-day onboarding, continuity, and 10% affiliate commission on clothing

**Starting state.** $309,000 revenue and $130,000 profit last year (42% margins), over 1,000 lifetime customers. Paid cold traffic went to a form with no headline, no value proposition and a 'get more info' button: 1,800 clicks produced 8 sales. No lead magnet, no video sales letter, no qualification. Six affiliates (found by a basic Google search and 40 emails) produced a third of the business. Most clients were grandfathered at $1,500/quarter or less, only a couple paid the $2,000/month tier, and no pricing was…

**Diagnosis.** Three constraints. (1) A leaky funnel - the bottleneck is conversion, not traffic, and it leaks because there is no reason to opt in and no qualification. (2) A missed gold mine - a channel already proven to work (6 affiliates, one-third of revenue, $2,500 of revenue per email sent) was being run at almost zero volume. (3) Pricing - no price anchor, no frictionless upsell from onboarding into continuity, and a premium brand delivered through a commodity sales process, so the frame breaks and conversion drops. He also places her at stage four of the scaling roadmap: identify and double down on…

**Intervention.**

- Funnel, step 1: add a lead magnet - a personalized style assessment (skin tone, body type, lifestyle) qualified on BANT plus income, since it is high-touch concierge work, not an ebook
- Funnel, step 2: install a VSSL - a 3-7 minute video that pre-frames the assessment and pre-sells the call; built by recording answers to the most common objections from sales recordings and sending it to every prospect in the funnel
- Funnel, step 3: qualify harder - BANT plus an income question in the intake form so unqualified buyers are filtered before she creates a personalized assessment
- Funnel, step 4: rewrite the headline and subheadline around the freebie: 'free lookbook to dress for your tone using your existing closet' (the 'using your existing closet' kills the biggest objection)
- Affiliates, step 1: build the list beyond matchmakers - private social clubs, executive coaches, high-end personal trainers, divorce attorneys - anyone whose customers are in the buying moment (recently divorced, newly single executives, wives whose husbands' dress does not match their status)
- Affiliates, step 2: send the emails - 400 in 30 days, 20 per day, no fancy software
- Affiliates, step 3: activate and retain - treat affiliates like customers, farm the relationship (dinners, events hosted for their customers, sponsorship that makes the affiliate look good)
- Pricing, step 1: introduce a highest-tier continuity option (about 10x) so the $2,000/month and $4,500/quarter look reasonable, keeping the anchor similar to the core offer with only one or two differences nobody cares about
- Pricing, step 2: make the back-end the default next step after onboarding ('you have already invested in your transformation, let's make sure it sticks')
- Pricing, step 3: keep pushing price until the conversion drop costs more than the price gain - the point of maximum profit is after the point of maximum conversion

**Result.** No measured results are given in this video - the fixes are presented as a plan. His estimates: the funnel rebuild (lead magnet, VSSL, qualification, headline) could give her 2-3x, and if only 10% of clients take a high-end anchor priced at 10x, it effectively doubles the revenue of the business.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Starting revenue and profit | **$309,000 revenue, $130,000 profit, 42% margins** |
| Funnel leak | **1,800 clicks to 8 sales** |
| Affiliate concentration | **six partners send a third of her entire business** |
| Affiliate expansion goal | **40 emails to date to 400 emails in 30 days (20/day), 6…** |
| Price anchor effect | **10% take at 10x price doubles revenue** |
| Estimated funnel fix effect | **2-3x** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Three moves, in this order. (1) Before buying more traffic, stop the leak: give a narrow, qualified free thing, add a short pre-call video built from recorded objections, and qualify with BANT so unqualified people never consume your delivery time. (2) Hunt the gold mine already inside the business - find the channel that produced outsized results and do 10x more of it (here: 40 emails had produced 6 partners worth a third of revenue, so the instruction was 400 emails in 30 days, plus a relationship owner to keep partners activated). (3) Then reprice: add a high anchor about 10x the core…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The affiliate numbers are the actionable part and are usually left out: 6 partners found by 40 emails produced one-third of revenue, worth $2,500 per email sent, so the prescribed move was 400 emails in 30 days at 20/day with a named list of adjacent business types (private social clubs, executive…
- The pricing mechanics are stated as a calculation: a 10x anchor taken by only 10% of clients doubles revenue, and the anchor should stay similar to the core offer with one or two differences nobody cares about.
- Unlike the other teardowns in this batch, this video gives no measured after-numbers - the results are projections (2-3x from the funnel fixes), so it should not be cited as a proven outcome.
- The transcript states '4% conversion to traffic' while the same passage gives 8 sales from 1,800 clicks (under 1%) - the two figures cannot both be right.

## If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview
`YZdE8U5eD_s` · https://youtu.be/YZdE8U5eD_s

*Harley Finkelstein (Shopify) explains how a snowboard shop's software became a ~$100B company: grow the pie rather than take a slice, be more generous than the incumbents (80/20 app store rev share, 20% in perpetuity to referral partners), and build for 100 years.*

### Case study

**Business.** Shopify - the e-commerce platform Tobi Lütke started in 2005 and Harley Finkelstein joined, told here by Harley (third-party case study in an interview, not a Hormozi teardown)

**Starting state.** In 2005 there were two ways to sell online: a marketplace, where you rent your customers, or enterprise software costing a couple of million dollars. Tobi Lütke, a programmer who had moved from Germany to Canada, wanted to build a snowboard shop on the internet and wrote his own software in Ruby on Rails rather than accept either option. Harley became one of the first merchants in 2006 (when the product was called Jaded Pixel) and joined the company around 2009 while also acting as its lawyer.

**Diagnosis.** The strategic constraint was not product but ecosystem and trust: a platform only wins if the people building on it make money, so the decisions that mattered were about being more generous than incumbents and letting partners carry distribution. Harley names three decisions from the first ten years: the app store and ecosystem (which gave 100% product-market fit across use cases and a distributed salesforce not on payroll), the Build-a-Business competition (which created new merchants and press), and Merchant Solutions (negotiating payment rates in aggregate as if they were the…

**Intervention.**

- Write the software rather than rent customers from a marketplace or pay millions for enterprise software
- Build an app store and set the developer revenue share at 80/20 when the incumbent (Apple's iOS store) was 70/30 - more generous than the incumbents
- Run the Build-a-Business competition with Tim Ferriss (launched 2010) with a $100,000 prize they did not yet have, generating new merchants and a New York Times article
- Pay referral partners 20% of what Shopify took, in perpetuity, turning agencies into a recurring cash-flow channel
- Use aggregate merchant size to negotiate payment gateway rates as if they were the second-largest retailer, then pass most of the benefit to merchants
- Hold to a merchant-obsessed mission as the single heuristic so thousands of employees can decide independently
- Think in decades - explicitly building a 100-year business, which meant patience over short-term extraction
- Divest businesses that are not 'main quests' (e.g. Shopify Fulfillment Network)
- Grow the pie rather than take a slice of it

**Result.** IPO in May 2015 on the NYSE at about a $1 billion valuation - roughly 1% of today's market cap. In 2022 Shopify did $5.6 billion of revenue while its merchants generated almost $200 billion of GMV, and ecosystem partners earned more than $6 billion. By the time of this interview Shopify was worth around $100 billion with 8,000-9,000 employees. Harley's recurring finding from interviewing entrepreneurs in their 80s and 90s (about 12 interviews, including Izzy Sharp of Four Seasons at 95) is that…

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Value of Shopify | **about $100 billion** |
| IPO | **May 2015, a $1B company then** |
| 2022 revenue vs merchant volume | **$5.6B revenue vs ~$200B GMV, partners made more than $6B** |
| App store rev share choice | **80/20 vs the incumbent's 70/30** |
| Referral partner share | **20% in perpetuity** |
| Headcount | **eight or nine thousand people at the company** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Build the ecosystem, not just the product: give partners a reason to sell for you (80/20 rev share when the incumbent offered 70/30; 20% in perpetuity to referrers), run a competition that manufactures new customers and press before you can afford the prize, and use aggregate scale to negotiate rates your individual customers could never get. Two operating rules underneath it: one simple heuristic everyone can apply independently (merchant obsessed), and a decade-long time horizon (a 100-year business) that lets you refuse anything that is not a main quest. The check on whether you are doing…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The partner economics are stated numerically and are the actionable part: 80/20 app store revenue share against the incumbent's 70/30, 20% in perpetuity to referral partners, and a $100,000 competition prize announced before they could afford it.
- The scale evidence is given: 2022 revenue $5.6B against ~$200B of merchant GMV and more than $6B earned by ecosystem partners, with an IPO in May 2015 at about $1B (roughly 1% of the value at interview time).
- This is an interview, not a teardown - the case study is Shopify's history as told by Harley Finkelstein, and there is no before/after intervention on a third-party business. Two figures are corrupted in the auto-captions ('100100 million' Series B valuation and Shopify's share of the 46 million…
